item.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
item.description:
The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump.

Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort.

  • Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up."
  • The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter.

Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present."

Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm.

  • Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

item.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
item.description:
The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump, multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios.

Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building, which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle.

  • The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building.

Driving the news: Axios could not immediately confirm when the closure will happen or how long it will be.

  • A resolution from the board, filed as evidence in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name.
  • The resolution cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building."

Zoom out: A second resolution filed on Monday listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name.

  • The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building."
  • It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump."

Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information."

  • But in that order, he said his injunction would not prevent "capital repair work," nor would it "categorically prohibit the Board from closing the Center should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion."

Catch up quick: The renovation project would address issues like corrosion and rehabilitating the building's iconic theaters and Grand Foyer, Axios previously reported.

  • The draft resolution proposes sending marquee events offsite, while continuing some programming at the REACH — an indoor–outdoor space.
  • Beyond infrastructure renovations, Trump ally and board member Paolo Zampolli outlined his luxury vision for the space to Axios' Cuneyt Dil, including expanding the outdoor park to create a "concert hub," and building a marina.

What we're watching: For now, those ideas aren't part of the board's resolution — but the center's future under Trump remains in flux, in part because of an ongoing legal challenge to the president's takeover.

  • And while Trump allies position him as the center's financial savior, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales plunged after the board of trustees voted to name the center after him.

Go deeper: Kennedy Center's survival depends on Trump, DOJ says in new filing

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
item.description:
President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use.

Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers.

  • The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue.

Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position."

  • Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads."
  • Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources.

Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies.

  • "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday.

Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates.

  • First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use.
  • Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities.
  • Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water.

"The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside."

Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource demands are known.

By the numbers: Fabrizio's polling shows voters are far more receptive to data center construction with conditions than unrestricted development.

  • Sixty-one percent of registered voters favor allowing construction with conditions, compared with 28% who favor prohibiting data centers altogether.
  • His polling also finds voters oppose additional data center construction without conditions by 65% to 24%.

The background: Fabrizio is a central player in Trump's midterm political operation, helping shape the polling and strategy guiding the GOP's campaign to retain control of Congress.

Yes, but: Trump remains an enthusiastic booster of data centers even as Republicans grapple with growing voter concerns about their local impact.

  • "I'm telling you, it's all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy, and it's the oil of the next 20, 25 years," Trump said Monday.

item.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
item.description:
Data: The Economist/YouGov; Chart: Avery Lotz

A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive.

The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war, tariffs or other top priorities. Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency.

By the numbers: "Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters.

  • Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%).
  • Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president.

Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high, per Gallup's trend, and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office.

  • The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans.
  • Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion.
  • Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion.

What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars."

  • Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government.

Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend, this month.

  • Some 35% of Americans approved of his performance, up from 33% in the late August poll, per Reuters.

Between the lines: The last thing many Republicans want, Axios' Marc Caputo reports, is for Trump to make the midterms a vote on his popularity (or lack thereof).

  • Still, Trump headlined both nights of the party's midterm convention in Dallas and pledged a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress — a plan that would cost more than $1 trillion.

Friction point: YouGov's polling found that a majority signaled they believe it's unlikely Trump actually follows through with the idea, which Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has said would require congressional approval.

  • More than four in 10 (41%) said he definitely wouldn't do it, while an additional 16% said he probably wouldn't. More said it was a bad idea (45%) than those who said it was a good idea (38%).

Methodology: This Economist-sponsored poll was taken September 11-14, 2026. Respondents were selected from YouGov's opt-in panel to be representative of adult U.S. citizens, and screened for voter registration. The margin of error is ± 3.3%.

Go deeper: Even some Republican voters sour on Trump

item.title: Massie moves to impeach Pete Hegseth over Iran War
item.description:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran.

Why it matters: The impeachment effort is a long shot in the GOP-controlled Congress, but Massie's resolution is privileged, meaning he can force a full House vote and put Republicans on the record over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war.

  • It's a dramatic escalation in the retiring lawmaker's months-long push to rein in the Trump administration's war powers. Massie did not give GOP leaders a heads-up on his plans.
  • The effort also comes after the House has repeatedly voted on efforts to constrain the administration's military campaign in Iran, including passing war powers resolutions in June and July directing the president to end U.S. hostilities with Tehran.
  • The House is slated to vote Tuesday on another war powers resolution on the Iran war effort.

Driving the news: Massie's resolution accuses Hegseth of carrying out orders to continue operations in Iran despite Congress' constitutional authority over war and its votes seeking to end the conflict.

  • Massie argued Hegseth's actions "frustrated Congress's ability to exercise its most solemn constitutional responsibility" and allowed an "unlawful war" to continue.
  • "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense," Massie said on the House floor.
  • The eight-article resolution also targets Hegseth over U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, including accusing him of illegally directing the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization.

Zoom out: Hegseth already faced a separate impeachment push from House Democrats, who introduced six articles against him in April that included allegations he waged an unauthorized war against Iran.

What's next: The House will have to take up the legislation within the next two legislative days, but GOP leaders could also move to vote on tabling the resolution instead.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to say that Massie didn't let GOP leaders know in advance about his plans.

item.title: Kennedy Center's attempt to put Trump's name on building blocked again by judge
item.description:
A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Kennedy Center's latest attempt to put President Trump's name on the performing arts center violated his earlier order blocking its renaming.

The big picture: The order came just before the Kennedy Center's board, now composed of Trump loyalists, is set to weigh shutting down the building for renovations that members argue must include Trump being "appropriately recognized" on the structure.

Driving the news: While Trump allies have argued the latest attempt to recognize Trump does not violate the law, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper said "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce."

  • Cooper ordered for Trump's name to be removed from the building in May, saying only Congress could change the name of the center that memorializes President John F. Kennedy.
  • The judge blocked the center from putting an inscription that read "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" on the main building or renaming the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."
  • Cooper wrote, "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Trump turns on the Supreme Court he helped build
item.description:
President Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after it struck down the president's mail-in voting order Monday night.

Why it matters: The president slammed the justices over rulings they've issued against him this year, suggesting without evidence that the three justices he appointed to the court are being controlled by the left.

What they're saying: "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "[T]hey are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won't be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal.
  • "It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history."
  • "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court - it will likely cost me dearly for years to come - but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!"

Zoom in: Trump unloaded on the court for striking down his birthright citizenship policy, in which the justices upheld that those born on American soil are citizens.

  • He also slammed their "horrible decision on Tariffs," after they ruled those unlawful earlier this year.
  • "Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," Trump wrote.

Between the lines: Without naming them, Trump criticized the three justices he appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

  • He explicitly praised Justices Alito and Thomas, who dissented in Monday's mail-in ballot ruling.
  • The Supreme Court could not be immediately reached for comment.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Trump DHS whistleblower alleges workers lied to access state voter data
item.description:
Department of Homeland Security employees were instructed to access state voter databases in ways a whistleblower alleges violate state law, according to a new report.

Why it matters: The policy signals the Trump administration's persistence in trying to root out purported voter fraud by any means necessary.

Driving the news: The whistleblower report, released by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), details a protected whistleblower disclosure that "reveals serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities" within DHS' Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate.

  • Employees have been asked to access sensitive voter information in state voter databases of people flagged by DHS as potential "unlawful voters," the report says.
  • The whistleblower says the process can result in errors involving naturalized U.S. citizens, potentially subjecting them to secondary customs screenings at airports, or criminal referrals to Homeland Security Investigations.

Zoom in: Some states, such as Virginia and Florida, require users signing onto the databases to legally confirm that they are the voter or an expressly authorized representative, meaning federal officers are effectively making false statements to access private records, the report says.

  • Officers are also under tremendous pressure to review and verify a person's citizenship status in 12 minutes and enter it into a law enforcement record.
  • The whistleblower says officers were told to rely on data they knew could be inaccurate, and employees' training on the new procedures amounted to a less-than-two-hour video.
  • As a result, U.S. citizens are being investigated through the initiative "without their knowledge or ability to correct erroneous data," the report says.

When officers questioned the practice, they were told individual officers would not be held personally liable for the searches, which the report says could indicate that the agency "is aware that the activity may be illegal."

What they're saying: "The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump's long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it," Schumer said in an emailed statement.

  • "This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans," he said. "Trump may try to steal this election, but we will make sure he can never be successful."
  • DHS and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Zoom out: The whistleblower report comes as the administration has been trying — and failing — to obtain sensitive voter information.

  • The administration is seeking information such as driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers, demanding that every state hand over voter registration lists, previous election ballots and access to voting equipment.
  • Federal courts have repeatedly rejected the DOJ's attempts to force states to turn over voter data, though litigation is ongoing in some states. 16 others voluntarily provided or agreed to provide voter files.

Attorneys suing the government say the requests raise privacy and security concerns and likely violate various state and federal laws.

  • Multiple audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud in America or proof that large numbers of noncitizens are voting.

What we're watching: Schumer and Padilla want DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to stop the initiative and brief Congress on its activities—it's unclear whether he will agree to do so.

Go deeper: DOJ's voter roll crusade hits a courthouse wall

Department of Homeland Security employees were instructed to access state voter databases in ways a whistleblower alleges violate state law, according to a new report.

Why it matters: The policy signals the Trump administration's persistence in trying to root out purported voter fraud by any means necessary.

Driving the news: The whistleblower report, released by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), details a protected whistleblower disclosure that "reveals serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities" within DHS' Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate.

  • Employees have been asked to access sensitive voter information in state voter databases of people flagged by DHS as potential "unlawful voters," the report says.
  • The whistleblower says the process can result in errors involving naturalized U.S. citizens, potentially subjecting them to secondary customs screenings at airports, or criminal referrals to Homeland Security Investigations.

Zoom in: Some states, such as Virginia and Florida, require users signing onto the databases to legally confirm that they are the voter or an expressly authorized representative, meaning federal officers are effectively making false statements to access private records, the report says.

  • Officers are also under tremendous pressure to review and verify a person's citizenship status in 12 minutes and enter it into a law enforcement record.
  • The whistleblower says officers were told to rely on data they knew could be inaccurate, and employees' training on the new procedures amounted to a less-than-two-hour video.
  • As a result, U.S. citizens are being investigated through the initiative "without their knowledge or ability to correct erroneous data," the report says.

When officers questioned the practice, they were told individual officers would not be held personally liable for the searches, which the report says could indicate that the agency "is aware that the activity may be illegal."

What they're saying: "The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump's long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it," Schumer said in an emailed statement.

  • "This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans," he said. "Trump may try to steal this election, but we will make sure he can never be successful."
  • DHS and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Attorneys suing the government say the requests raise privacy and security concerns and likely violate various state and federal laws.

What we're watching: Schumer and Padilla want DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to stop the initiative and brief Congress on its activities—it's unclear whether he will agree to do so.

item.title: Cities challenge Trump immigration rule over public benefits access
item.description:
New York City and five other Democratic-led local governments sued the Department of Homeland Security to block a new Trump administration rule they say will drive immigrants and mixed-status families away from public benefits they can legally receive.

Why it matters: The cities warn the rule could drive hundreds of thousands out of health, food and housing programs, worsening public health, increasing homelessness and shifting millions of dollars in costs to local hospitals and governments.

What they're saying: "The federal government has waged a campaign of violence and terror," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a Monday news conference.

  • "People could die as a result of these changes," he said. "… The data is clear: denying people services does not erase their need; it compounds it, generating a greater cost to our system that will be placed on the backs of working people for years to come. Nothing about this rule will reduce waste or keep Americans safer or improve New Yorkers' lives. It is simply a vehicle for confusion and a vehicle for cruelty."
  • The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

The other side: "Let's get this straight, sanctuary states are terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs," a DHS spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "We're shaking in our boots over this supposedly terrible outcome. This is the ideological contortion required by left-wing leaders to justify their defrauding of the American taxpayer at the hands of illegal criminals."
  • "DHS has heard for months from the trusted journalists at CNN and others that illegal aliens weren't using these very same welfare programs. So, which is it?"

Catch up quick: The administration's rule takes effect this week and gives immigration officers broader discretion to deny green cards and visas based on immigrants' use of public benefits.

  • Plaintiffs say the change abandons a century-old standard that limited who was considered a "public charge" to people who are "primarily dependent" on government cash assistance.
  • The cities and counties argue the new rule will deter immigrant families from using Medicaid, SNAP, and housing assistance programs.
  • New York City, Chicago, San Francisco and Seattle, along with Santa Clara County, California, and King County, Washington, filed the suit.

Zoom in: DHS estimates over 950,000 people might disenroll or decline to enroll in public benefits, though the plaintiffs allege that estimate probably understates the effect.

  • The final rule could potentially cause U.S. citizen family members to withdraw from benefit programs.

Worth noting: The plaintiffs also say that the policy alert should have gone through a formal notice and comment because, despite being labeled guidance, it functions as a binding substantive rule.

  • The rule follows a Republican reconciliation package in 2025 that limited legal immigrants' access to health insurance.

The bottom line: The cities and counties argue the new rule gives immigration officers too much discretion, punishes lawful benefit use and will discourage potentially millions of people — including U.S. citizen children — from seeking food, health, housing and education assistance.

Go deeper: The health impact of Trump's new "public charge" rule

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from the Department of Homeland Security.

item.title: Scoop: U.S. attacked Iranian boats trying to seize Navy drone
item.description:
The U.S. military destroyed two Iranian small boats Monday after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps tried to steal a Navy drone patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. officials told Axios.

Why it matters: The unusual incident shows how efforts to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues direct confrontation with Iran.

  • The U.S. military initially didn't disclose the strike, and Iranian media presented it as a drone strike on "fishing boats."

Driving the news: According to Iranian media, two fishing boats were struck Monday off the coast of the port city of Kargan and near Larak Island in Hormozgan province.

  • Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor for security affairs, attributed the strike to the U.S. military.
  • Nafisi said an unspecified number of fishermen were missing and that search-and-rescue operations were underway, according to Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency.

Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the IRGC used the boats to try to capture a naval drone that the U.S. military uses to patrol the Strait of Hormuz.

  • After U.S. forces identified the attempt, an American drone fired two missiles at the boats, destroying them and killing most of those on board.

What they are saying: U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure, saying "Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a U.S. unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after CENTCOM forcefully responded."

  • "The surface drone remains under U.S. operational control," Hawkins said.

State of play: The incident took place as the U.S. attempts to protect increased commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil flows remain below prewar levels.

  • A U.S. official said the U.S. military and Gulf countries have begun conducting daytime transits of tankers through the strait and not only night time as was the case in recent month.
  • As fighting with the Houthis in the Red Sea escalates, Saudi Arabia has significantly increased the number of oil tankers it sends through the strait, a U.S. official said.
  • U.S. forces have also expanded the mine-cleared parts of the strait's middle shipping lane.

By the numbers: An average of 40 ships now transit the strait daily under U.S. military guidance and protection.

  • Roughly 14 million barrels of oil are exported through the waterway daily, a U.S. official said.
  • Over the last week, several tankers carrying liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas have also transited the strait.

item.title: House Democrats face divisions on Russian sanctions bill
item.description:
House Democratic leadership is vocally opposing a Russia sanctions bill set to come to a vote this week, but not all of their members are comfortable taking that stance just yet.

Why it matters: Republicans will reportedly need some Democratic votes to make up for defections from their isolationist wing and pass the measure.

  • At issue for many Democrats is that the bill, named in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would allow the Trump administration to impose up to 100% tariffs on the five top importers of Russian oil.
  • That has forced Democrats to choose between two issues that have become shibboleths for their party: support for Ukraine and opposition to giving President Trump more power to set trade policy.

State of play: Reps. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Richard Neal (D-Mass.) — the ranking members of the House Foreign Affairs, Joint Economic and Ways & Means committees, respectively — announced their opposition to the bill in a joint statement last week.

  • "House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good," they said.
  • "This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable."

Yes, but: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), an arch-centrist who often breaks with party leadership, told Axios last week he is "almost certainly going to be a 'yes' on the bill.

  • "I think the sanctions [are good] but I am also generally supportive of tariffs," said Golden.
  • The Maine Democrat has been his party's lone cheerleader for many of Trump's more controversial protectionist trade measures.

Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio), the co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus, told Axios she is "reviewing [the bill] very carefully" and "working with our Ukraine Caucus."

  • "I think it's important to send Russia a message that she needs to stand down," Kaptur added.
  • Rep. Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), the other Democratic co-chair of the Ukraine Caucus, told Axios last week he is going to "see what it looks like" and that his vote "depends on exact wording."

Between the lines: Meeks and former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), another staunch Ukraine supporter, tried to get amendments to the bill to make the trade language more palatable.

  • The Republican-controlled House Rules Committee rejected those proposed changes Monday and advanced the bill to a procedural vote on the House floor.
  • The bill passed in an overwhelmingly bipartisan 86-11 Senate vote last month and is supported by the White House, but its momentum has slowed in the House.

item.title: Scoop: Top House Democrat launches investigation into Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding
item.description:
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is investigating a Russian oligarch's reported financial involvement in a celebration related to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Garcia is poised to be Congress' lead investigator if Democrats retake the House. This probe offers a pretty good hint of the direction he'll go in that role.

  • "Oversight Democrats are investigating the numerous ways in which the Trump family have sought to enrich themselves on the basis of their proximity to President Donald Trump," Garcia stated in a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
  • In a separate letter to Trump Jr., Garcia wrote that ProPublica's reporting on Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev's role in funding the event "may be the most serious allegation against you to date."

Driving the news: Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, provided hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of expenses for the May party in the Bahamas, according to ProPublica.

  • Kremlev is close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his boxing organization is financed by Russian state-owned energy company Gazprom.
  • The oligarch paid for one of the two private islands where the event was held and a fireworks show, according to ProPublica, despite Trump Jr.'s estimated $300 million net worth.

A Trump Jr. spokesperson did not dispute the payments to ProPublica, telling the outlet Kremlev is "a personal friend of Don," but "not someone he has a business relationship with."

  • Kremlev's press office told ProPublica the two met "a couple of years ago" and "have a friendly relationship," and that he has "never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances."
  • Trump Jr.'s wife, Bettina Anderson, said in a statement on Instagram that it is "unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister," adding, "Friendship doesn't require a political motive."

President Trump said in a statement to Axios shared by the White House press office that he has "no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn't pay for Don and Bettina's wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding."

  • "It was an 'afterparty' given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party," he added.
  • A representative for Trump Jr. did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Kremlev.

The latest: In his letter to Wiles, Garcia wrote that he wants all "documents, records, and communications between the White House and Mr. Donald Trump, Jr., concerning Mr. Umar Kremlev," including any warnings about his ties to Putin.

  • He asked whether Trump Jr. has a security clearance, whether he disclosed his ties to Kremlev to the White House, and if President Trump's absence from the ceremony was related to the oligarch's involvement.
  • "Any possible foreign entanglement deserves close scrutiny," Garcia wrote, citing reports that Trump Jr. is a key political adviser to his father.

Garcia requested Trump Jr. turn over an array of documents, including a full guest list, dates of contact between him and Kremlev, and any communications he has had with the White House or intelligence officials about Kremlev.

  • He also wants records of "all purchases made for your wedding by foreign nationals and others on your behalf," and gifts he received from foreign nationals or "those with close ties to adversaries of the United States."
  • He asked Trump Jr. if Mr. Kremlev has ever provided him "anything of value in exchange for favorable treatment by the U.S. government or information about the Trump Administration."

Between the lines: As the top minority party member on the panel, Garcia is currently stuck making voluntary requests for information, which can easily be shrugged off by the administration and Trump family members.

  • That all changes if Democrats win the House and he obtains the Oversight Committee gavel next January: He would be able to compel potential witnesses to testify and turn over documents.

item.title: Baal out: Top diplomat's worry about pagan god elicits eye rolls
item.description:
The second-most powerful man at the State Department put the brakes on a U.S. international exhibit featuring a bull statue because he worried it might look like Baal, a pagan god some associate with Satanic child sacrifice. Why it matters: The anecdote illustrates the quirky interests of Deputy Secretary of State Chris Landau, according to department critics, who say he spends too much time on social media focusing on the unimportant.

Zoom in: The issue revolves around an international exposition next year in Belgrade, Serbia, where the U.S. plans to feature a statue of a bucking bull at an exhibit celebrating the American West.

  • On Aug. 19, at 4:15 p.m., Landau sent an email to staffers about it: "I remain somewhat concerned by the Golden Bull imagery! Did a quick internet search and don't want it to become a distraction. The golden calf from the Bible is often portrayed as a golden bull."
  • Providing hyperlinked footnotes and images of golden bull worship, Landau explored the ancient history of Baal as well as the "Modern Cultural Comparisons."
  • "The imagery of a golden bull or calf is frequently invoked metaphorically today," he wrote. "For instance, critics and commentators sometimes compare modern financial fixations—typified by the famous Charging Bull statue on Wall Street to the ancient worship of material idols."

Behind the scenes: The email, which was forwarded to multiple officials, elicited eyerolls and snickers inside the State Department.

  • The bull statue was put on hold as State officials spent the last few weeks debating how to make it both interesting and non-Satanic.
  • "It's just totally weird stuff and it's really indicative of the guy," a State Department official said.
  • "Literally, no one thinks about Baal unless they're spending way too much time online, which Landau is," a different U.S. official lamented.
  • "It's like an episode of Veep. Someone should tell him this is a Western bull, not a Near East bull," a third U.S. official said.
  • Landau declined to comment through a State Department spokesperson.
Screenshot: Chris Landau email

Between the lines: Mentions of Baal spiked this year amid a wave of online antisemitism linked to Iranian propaganda and conspiracy theories about the Jeffrey Epstein files.

  • In late January, a conspiracy theory spread on X that Epstein had a bank account named Baal, a name some online commentators have linked to child sacrifice. A Yahoo fact check found that the "Baal" reference was actually an AI scanning error for "bank."
  • Weeks later, just before the U.S. and Israel unleashed their Feb. 28 bombing campaign, Iranian officials organized rallies across the country where people burned effigies of Baal. The regime specifically linked the symbol to Epstein and an alleged cult of child sacrifice.
  • Around this time, right-wing podcaster Candace Owens made an episode called "BAAL SO HARD: The Epstein Files." It has nearly 3 million views.

Zoom out: Landau became a State Department online sensation during President Trump's first term while serving as ambassador to Mexico, according to Slate.

  • His private account, @ChrisLandauUSA, has nearly 248,000 followers, where he posts sometimes-quirky content like AI-animated sweet potatoes.
  • In March, Landau was criticized for using his official account to reply neutrally to a bigoted account complaining that passports now look like a "zogpass," a reference to the antisemitic acronym "ZOG" that stands for a "Zionist Occupied Government" controlled by Jews.
Screenshot: Chris Landau email

Friction point: Landau has had repeated internal dustups within the Trump administration, sources tell Axios.

  • He repeatedly clashed with Paolo Zampolli, a friend of President Trump, who appointed Zampolli as U.S. Special Representative for Global Partnerships.
  • In June, other U.S. officials accused Landau of "going rogue" concerning the administration's position on exiled Venezuelan leader Maria Corina Machado, Axios first reported.
  • Last week, the Daily Mail reported Landau almost orchestrated the firing of another Trump ally, Gavin Wax, from his State Department post over a lunch Wax had with Serbian officials.

The backstory: Wax's boss, Undersecretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah Rogers, is technically in charge of planning the exposition in Serbia next year. But a senior U.S. official said her role was "hijacked" by Landau.

  • "This is not the D's job," the official said, referring to the single initial nickname for the Deputy Secretary of State used at Foggy Bottom. "This was just regular planning until he stepped in."
  • Landau, the official noted, was quick to pooh-pooh one item featured at prior expositions: "No one cares about the moonrock," Landau has said repeatedly.
  • For the American West exhibit, the department's director of art in embassies, Erin Scavino, recommended featuring a mechanical bucking bull that people could ride. But that idea was scrapped after department officials determined that liability exposure in Serbia was too great.

What they're not saying: Rogers also declined to comment through a State Department spokesperson. Wax and Scavino couldn't be reached.

What's next: Expo 2027 Belgrade is scheduled to run from May 15 to Aug. 15, 2027.

  • "We'll have the bull sorted out by then," one of the officials said. "And it won't be Satanic."

Why it matters: The anecdote illustrates the quirky interests of Deputy Secretary of State Chris Landau, according to department critics, who say he spends too much time on social media focusing on the unimportant.

Zoom in: The issue revolves around an international exposition next year in Belgrade, Serbia, where the U.S. plans to feature a statue of a bucking bull at an exhibit celebrating the American West.

  • On Aug. 19, at 4:15 p.m., Landau sent an email to staffers about it: "I remain somewhat concerned by the Golden Bull imagery! Did a quick internet search and don't want it to become a distraction. The golden calf from the Bible is often portrayed as a golden bull."
  • Providing hyperlinked footnotes and images of golden bull worship, Landau explored the ancient history of Baal as well as the "Modern Cultural Comparisons."
  • "The imagery of a golden bull or calf is frequently invoked metaphorically today," he wrote. "For instance, critics and commentators sometimes compare modern financial fixations—typified by the famous Charging Bull statue on Wall Street to the ancient worship of material idols."

Behind the scenes: The email, which was forwarded to multiple officials, elicited eyerolls and snickers inside the State Department.

  • The bull statue was put on hold as State officials spent the last few weeks debating how to make it both interesting and non-Satanic.
  • "It's just totally weird stuff and it's really indicative of the guy," a State Department official said.
  • "Literally, no one thinks about Baal unless they're spending way too much time online, which Landau is," a different U.S. official lamented.
  • "It's like an episode of Veep. Someone should tell him this is a Western bull, not a Near East bull," a third U.S. official said.
  • Landau declined to comment through a State Department spokesperson.

item.title: Why a swift AI pause is unlikely: No one trusts AI companies
item.description:
Most agree the AI industry needs oversight.

  • The critical barrier: Few really trust the industry, or the safety advocates who come from inside the house.

Why it matters: Factions in the Trump administration, business executives wary of competitive threats, and advocates for cheaper, more customizable "open" models fear that new regulatory hurdles will offer frontier AI companies too much power.

What they're saying: "I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence," Gavin Baker, a top tech investor and commentator on the AI race, said Sunday on X.

  • Baker said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was surely sincere when he proposed new AI regulatory proposals in an essay Saturday, although the moves "would be good for his business over the long-term."

Catch up quick: Four leading U.S. AI companies endorsed a potential pause in AI development this weekend after a series of troubling hacking incidents and awe-inducing displays of new model capabilities.

  • The suggested pause caused a dip in global markets Monday as investors pondered what a slowdown in AI, one of the few reliable engines of economic growth this year, would do to economies around the world.
  • Any hope of quick action extending from that fragile unity quickly shattered as critics spoke up and made clear just how much they distrust frontier AI players.

AI distrust, explained

Here are the key factors shaping that distrust, which are poised to delay the kind of "all-hands-on-deck" response many want.

💰Money: Anthropic stands alone in the history of capitalism, a company whose leaders are so concerned with safety that it broke away from OpenAI. Its employees, up to the CEO, honestly believe its product is so dangerous that there's a chance it could destroy humanity.

  • And yet, as soon as this week, it's expected to file for what many expect will be the biggest IPO of all time, seeking to raise $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation.
  • Picture Oppenheimer meeting with sell-side analysts and you get a window into the Dr. Strangelove of it all. That duality — dire warnings and fundraising based on promises of AI Valhalla — continues to sow confusion.

⚠️ Safety: A group of AI obsessives and technologists for years have spent vast sums financing research and organizations dedicated to AI safety. The problem is that many critics see some of that work as lacking in substance, too focused on the probability of end-of-the-world scenarios.

  • Another issue is how closely aligned some safety research organizations are to frontier AI labs. Many of those organizations employ former OpenAI and Anthropic employees, accept free tokens (for analysis) and take funding from organizations focused on existential risk.
  • Anthropic has pointed to METR, which conducted the evaluation of the HuggingFace incident at OpenAI, as a possible third-party evaluator. But industry skeptics point to a laundry list of financial and personal ties between the two companies as a non-starter for competitors.
  • To the extent top U.S. AI companies embrace self-regulation, an increasingly likely possibility, finding third-party organizations that are viewed as truly independent will be a challenge. While self-regulation has worked in plenty of industries, it has a mixed track record in tech, with Meta's largely toothless Oversight Board as exhibit A.

📊 Business: A coterie of business leaders, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, have embraced open weight AI systems, which are generally cheaper and offer companies the chance to build and customize proprietary models with their own data.

  • Most of the best open models were made by Chinese startups, and some U.S. companies are using them to save money and protect themselves from potential competition from frontier AI companies.
  • Given expectations that China would be unlikely to cooperate with any voluntary pause or slowdown, any attempt to bring AI systems under control could lead to a ban or restrictions on usage of Chinese models, something that might cause many U.S. businesses to revolt.

🏛️ Politics: Top administration officials, including White House AI advisor David Sacks, have repeatedly dismissed the push for regulation and oversight as a classic attempt at "regulatory capture."

  • A slowdown brokered by the frontier labs could freeze their lead in place, an incentive that Sacks and venture capitalist Bill Gurley have pointed to a number of times.

What we're watching: Who steps into the vacuum.

  • While the industry squabbles over which evaluators are most honest and most independent, some key figures with Washington ties tell Axios they're thinking of starting their own shops to potentially fill the void.

The bottom line: Getting four top AI labs — Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Google — to agree on anything is a huge leap forward for the kind of regulation many AI proponents believe the industry desperately needs.

  • But a lack of trust in the companies makes swift oversight unlikely.

Maria Curi contributed reporting.

item.title: "I am the Hoax Buster": Trump's war on AI doomers gets personal
item.description:
President Trump declared war on the AI safety panic Monday, dismissing the industry's apocalyptic warnings as part of a "sick conspiracy" to sabotage America and his legacy.

Why it matters: Trump is rewriting a complex, years-long debate over AI's dangers in the partisan grammar that has defined MAGA for a decade — hoaxes, conspiracies, traitors and, at the center of it all, one man.

  • "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT," Trump wrote in a barrage of pro-AI Truth Social posts, where he accused Democrats of stoking the panic.

State of play: Monday marked a sharp escalation in the administration's long-standing opposition to AI regulation, as Trump recast the safety debate in starkly personal terms.

  • Trump explicitly placed AI doomerism in the same bucket as the Russia investigation, climate change and his impeachments — the latest entry in a catalog of "hoaxes" that has also included the Epstein files and the affordability crisis.
  • He turned his fire on the AI leaders urging restraint, questioning why CEOs would seek regulations that could cripple their own companies and arguing that any slowdown would squander America's lead over China.

The intrigue: Trump's campaign against AI doomerism then spilled onto the stage of the "All In Summit" in Los Angeles, where Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a call from the president in the middle of a live interview.

  • Addressing thousands of tech executives, investors and founders on speakerphone, Trump dismissed fears of an AI takeover as a "hoax" and assured the crowd that "the robots will not be taking over."
Screenshot via Truth Social

Between the lines: Trump is grafting his own political grievances onto a counter-narrative already taking hold among his Silicon Valley allies: that the AI panic is manufactured.

  • David Sacks, Trump's influential AI adviser and "All In" podcaster, has portrayed AI alarmism as the work of a well-funded "Doomer Industrial Complex" that includes former Biden officials.
  • As the latest warnings exploded across social media last week, Sacks and his co-hosts suggested the backlash was a coordinated "psyop" tied to election season and the growing threat from open-source AI.

The big picture: Critics question how Trump, an 80-year-old populist who famously shuns email, became such an evangelist for AI. The answer lies in an AI narrative almost perfectly calibrated to Trump's instincts:

  • A race with China that America is currently winning.
  • A historic buildout of data centers, chip fabs and power plants — physical monuments to investment and growth.
  • Tech titans competing for his ear and influence.
  • A booming stock market.
  • A futuristic vision of American supremacy built on speed, scale and technological might.
  • And now, a familiar foil: an elite "expert" class telling him no.

The bottom line: Trump has been an AI accelerationist from the start.

  • What's new is the degree to which he now sees the AI boom as his boom — and the safety revolt as an attempt to deny him his place in history.

item.title: Supreme Court strikes down USPS mail-in voting rule
item.description:
The Supreme Court struck down the U.S. Postal Service's rule restructuring mail-in voting Monday, halting a major Trump administration priority.

The big picture: The 7-2 decision is a major win for voting rights advocates and the states that challenged the administration's plan; it also reverses the Supreme Court's earlier green light for President Trump's mail-in voting order.

  • The justices' prior unsigned order allowing the rule to proceed was not a ruling on the merits — but this time around, they decided the government is "unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge."
  • The rule would require states to submit lists of eligible voters to USPS, and the agency would then verify that those voters were receiving mail-in ballots before sending them out. The rule also had strict requirements on envelope design.

Driving the news: While the court rejected the administration's stance, at least one concurring justice disagreed on the merits of the case.

  • Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion with fellow Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority" but that applying the proposed rules would be "arbitrary and capricious" for the midterm elections as state and local officials "do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule."
  • Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented in a separate opinion.
  • In their opinion, they called the filings claiming harm by some plaintiffs "cryptic" and that the USPS has the authority to implement a rule because Congress has empowered it to do so.

Zoom out: The decision is likely the final say on the rule during this election cycle, with even U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani saying from the bench earlier this month that it was unclear how the government would implement the plans with November just around the corner.

  • Steven Monteith, executive vice president at the Postal Service, said in a declaration filed Sept. 3 that the agency continues to make "refinements" to the portal, which he predicted would be available for "voluntary use by sometime next week."
  • He added that under Talwani's restraining order, USPS was not mandating design review for state mail but has made review available for states that want to "voluntarily submit" envelopes to ensure they comply with the rule.
  • The case has been full of legal twists and turns, with Talwani blocking key parts of the rule last month and a second judge doing the same earlier this week.

Friction point: While the administration has dismissed concerns, a USPS whistleblower recently alleged that the agency defied court orders and rushed to build out the new ballot system, putting thousands of mail ballots at risk.

  • The whistleblower said the Postal Service built the system in weeks, not the nine months to a year typically needed for a project of this complexity, Axios' Andrew Pantazi and Donica Phifer reported.

The bottom line: The rule is just one front in the myriad ways the administration has tried—at times, unsuccessfully—to reshape elections, as seen in attempts to obtain state voter rolls and redraw congressional maps.

  • Some of those efforts have been snuffed out in the courtroom, while others could have real impacts in November.

Editor's note: This story was updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: "Look for other ways to get attention": House Dems face new Trump impeachment blowup
item.description:
Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) is facing swift and intense anger from his Democratic colleagues after announcing plans to force a vote to impeach President Trump this week.

Why it matters: This is a messaging headache the party did not need going into the House's last week in session before midterm Election Day, frustrated House Democrats told Axios.

  • "It's fucked up," said a senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid criticism of a fellow Democrat.
  • Fumed a second lawmaker: "There's a reason why Al Green isn't coming back. This is exactly what people don't want. People want us focusing on affordability and AI, not on starting this futile impeachment game."
  • Green said in an interview: "People are dying, and they are talking about strategy."

Driving the news: Green said in a letter to Trump, which he cc'd to fellow members of Congress, that he will exercise his privilege to force a House impeachment vote "during the legislative business of September 14-17."

  • He said the vote will be based on the killings of Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by federal immigration officers.
  • "You are condoning, supporting, and covering up these unjustified killings. The American people deserve more from their leader," Green wrote to Trump.

Between the lines: Green, who lost his primary to fellow Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) in May, has positioned himself as one of the president's most obdurate critics in Congress.

  • He was escorted out of Trump's speech to a joint session of Congress last year and his State of the Union this year, both times for heckling.
  • He mounted rogue efforts to impeach Trump in 2017, 2018, and twice last year, but all of his attempts were quashed in bipartisan procedural votes.

What we're hearing: A third House Democrat vented that "Rep. Green appears to only be thinking about himself. Not about strategy. Not about building a coalition."

  • "We need serious people in our caucus focused on the mission: flipping the House to end this national nightmare," the lawmaker said.
  • A fourth House Democrat told Axios: "Sure, he will excite the non-strategic activist crowd. But why is he empowering Trump?"
  • "Every time you swing and miss at the guy, his approval rating goes up. Look for other ways to get attention," they added.

Between the lines: Others, including party leadership, are brushing the vote off as a distraction.

  • "Another day, another Al Green moment," a Democratic leadership source said.
  • A fifth House Democrat told Axios: "Obviously, he is looking to keep his profile up. Don't think this fundamentally changes anything."

The other side: "Where is the fight in the Democrats that are speaking anonymously? ... They don't have the courage to stand up and face me," Green told Axios.

  • "I would challenge any one of them or all of them to debate me." he added.
  • Green also pushed back on the argument that his impeachment vote is pointless: "Rosa Parks didn't know she was going to win. In fact, Rosa Parks knew she wouldn't win the night she took a seat on that bus."
  • "Not one of them indicated that the president's actions are not impeachable, yet these Democrats are going to vote to stall and/or prevent the president from being impeached," the Texas Democrat said.

The intrigue: Some Democrats who privately dislike Green's impeachment push likely will vote for it anyway for fear of backlash from the party base.

  • "If he forces it, I have no choice but to vote for it," acknowledged the third House Democrat.
  • There are also some true believers like Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), who is also leaving Congress next year after losing his primary and told Axios: "Obviously I will be voting for [it]."

What to watch: While Democrats can easily shrug off this vote as a farce, they will face a very real dilemma next year if they retake control of one or both chambers of Congress, as Axios previously reported.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is toeing a careful line on the issue, saying in a CNN interview last month, "We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out."
  • His public ambivalence reflects genuine divisions among House Democrats as to whether it is worth trying to impeach Trump a third time.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) is facing swift and intense anger from his Democratic colleagues after announcing plans to force a vote to impeach President Trump this week.

Why it matters: This is a messaging headache the party did not need going into the House's last week in session before midterm Election Day, frustrated House Democrats told Axios.

  • "It's fucked up," said a senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid criticism of a fellow Democrat.
  • Fumed a second lawmaker: "There's a reason why Al Green isn't coming back. This is exactly what people don't want. People want us focusing on affordability and AI, not on starting this futile impeachment game."
  • Green said in an interview: "People are dying, and they are talking about strategy."

Driving the news: Green said in a letter to Trump, which he cc'd to fellow members of Congress, that he will exercise his privilege to force a House impeachment vote "during the legislative business of September 14-17."

  • He said the vote will be based on the killings of Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by federal immigration officers.
  • "You are condoning, supporting, and covering up these unjustified killings. The American people deserve more from their leader," Green wrote to Trump.

Between the lines: Green, who lost his primary to fellow Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) in May, has positioned himself as one of the president's most obdurate critics in Congress.

  • He was escorted out of Trump's speech to a joint session of Congress last year and his State of the Union this year, both times for heckling.
  • He mounted rogue efforts to impeach Trump in 2017, 2018, and twice last year, but all of his attempts were quashed in bipartisan procedural votes.

What we're hearing: A third House Democrat vented that "Rep. Green appears to only be thinking about himself. Not about strategy. Not about building a coalition."

  • "We need serious people in our caucus focused on the mission: flipping the House to end this national nightmare," the lawmaker said.
  • A fourth House Democrat told Axios: "Sure, he will excite the non-strategic activist crowd. But why is he empowering Trump?"
  • "Every time you swing and miss at the guy, his approval rating goes up. Look for other ways to get attention," they added.

Between the lines: Others, including party leadership, are brushing the vote off as a distraction.

  • "Another day, another Al Green moment," a Democratic leadership source said.
  • A fifth House Democrat told Axios: "Obviously, he is looking to keep his profile up. Don't think this fundamentally changes anything."

The other side: "Where is the fight in the Democrats that are speaking anonymously? ... They don't have the courage to stand up and face me," Green told Axios.

  • "I would challenge any one of them or all of them to debate me." he added.
  • Green also pushed back on the argument that his impeachment vote is pointless: "Rosa Parks didn't know she was going to win. In fact, Rosa Parks knew she wouldn't win the night she took a seat on that bus."
  • "Not one of them indicated that the president's actions are not impeachable, yet these Democrats are going to vote to stall and/or prevent the president from being impeached," the Texas Democrat said.

The intrigue: Some Democrats who privately dislike Green's impeachment push likely will vote for it anyway for fear of backlash from the party base.

  • "If he forces it, I have no choice but to vote for it," acknowledged the third House Democrat.
  • There are also some true believers like Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), who is also leaving Congress next year after losing his primary and told Axios: "Obviously I will be voting for [it]."

What to watch: While Democrats can easily shrug off this vote as a farce, they will face a very real dilemma next year if they retake control of one or both chambers of Congress, as Axios previously reported.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is toeing a careful line on the issue, saying in a CNN interview last month, "We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out."
  • His public ambivalence reflects genuine divisions among House Democrats as to whether it is worth trying to impeach Trump a third time.

item.title: Thune sees role for Congress on AI — Trump does not
item.description:
Majority Leader John Thune is asserting Congress' prerogative to act on AI — but he's urging a "light touch" even in the face of "consequential risks."

Why it matters: On his first day back after a five-week break, Thune (R-S.D.) outlined his vision for congressional action on an issue President Trump has dismissed as a "hoax."

  • "Congress has a job to do," Thune said.
  • "I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI," Thune told reporters when asked if he believes AI poses an existential threat to humanity. He added, "Guardrails there make sense to me" about cutting-edge, frontier AI models.
  • But Thune also said that "there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there."
  • Driving the news: An AI panic is rippling through Congress, but mostly on the Democratic side, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) calling to "slow down the pace of development" of AI to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome.
  • Publicly, Trump is professing not to be concerned and insists that he should have the sole authority to regulate AI.
  • "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he posted on his Truth Social account Monday morning.

Zoom out: Republicans aren't questioning Trump's ability to lead the country's approach to AI regulation, but they are suggesting that Congress has a role to play.

  • And they aren't ruling out legislation.
  • "So we may need to do something," Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said. "But there are existing guardrails, and corporate responsibility is a big part of this."

Zoom in: Thune said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) on Saturday night about their AI bill, which would force companies creating frontier AI models to guard against catastrophic risks and submit to federal oversight.

  • Thune said he has been working with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to reintroduce the bill "hopefully soon."
  • House GOP leaders, meanwhile, have given no indication they plan to keep the chamber in session after this week to work on AI-related legislation.
  • "I don't know that staying in more weeks in September is going to be the catalyst for that," Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), the lead Republican on the FRONTIER Act, told Axios.

Between the lines: Before this weekend, much of the AI debate in Washington — and in Senate races — was focused on data centers and the amount of electricity they consume.

  • Republicans, as well as the White House, are eager to prove to voters that they won't face higher utility bills caused by data centers and their need for megawatts.
  • Thune left open the possibility of the Senate voting on a version of the House's Ratepayer Protection Act, which is aimed at ensuring communities are not forced to pay more for increased energy use by data centers.
  • The House is expected to vote on the bill Tuesday.

What we're hearing: Thune is uniquely prepared for the AI discussion, having worked on AI legislation for years.

  • Before he joined leadership, he chaired the Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over AI.
  • His familiarity with the complicated and evolving subject comes in contrast to many lawmakers who have little experience with AI.
  • Johnson even said on a podcast he has never used an AI chatbot. "Congress is not the expert on this subject because we are not in the frontier labs with them," he told reporters Monday evening.

The bottom line: Thune is signaling he's open to some regulation that wouldn't stifle innovation.

  • "I think you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated," he told reporters.
  • "I do think we are in a race with China, and I think there's huge upside, obviously, with AI as well."

item.title: Trump's $5,000 checks get chilly Senate GOP reception
item.description:
Data: OMB; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Senate Republicans are doubtful — and, in some cases, dismissive — of President Trump's proposal to give Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans keep control of Congress.

Why it matters: Trump's proposal isn't dead on arrival. But Republicans aren't exactly lining up behind it either.

  • "I am withholding judgment on the bill until I see their list of pay-fors," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said. "I don't support going and borrowing $1.2 trillion to be able to write the checks."
  • "I would need to see details on it," Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) said.
  • Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said he wasn't sure about the mechanics of the proposal but that he's "also worrying about $40 trillion in debt."

"You know, there's no specific proposal out there," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "And obviously, however that were to come together, Congress would have a big role in determining."

Zoom in: There are two massive unknowns about the "Trump Dividend" that the president promised in Dallas last week: eligibility and price tag.

  • Vice President Vance has suggested that wealthy Americans wouldn't receive the payment.
  • If every "every adult citizen in the United States" were eligible, as Trump suggested, it could cost some $1.3 trillion.
  • That would be more than three times what the U.S. collects annually from tariffs and other customs duties and fees.

The intrigue: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who frequently defers to Trump, said Sunday that Congress would have to approve the payments.

  • Asked in NBC's "Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said, "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else."
  • Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) told Axios: "Well, if it happens, I'm recommending to people that they put it away in order to pay for the additional inflation. We will see."

— Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed reporting for this story.

item.title: McConnell returns to Capitol after 3-month absence
item.description:
Sen. Mitch McConnell voted at the U.S. Capitol on Monday for the first time in three months after being hospitalized in June.

Why it matters: The Kentucky Republican's return could finally unjam the farm bill — and put some MAGA world rumors to rest about his ability to do the job.

  • McConnell arrived in a wheelchair and spoke briefly to reporters, joking that after years of avoiding their questions, he "wasn't sure how many of you would be here today. But I'm glad to see you. It's time to get back to work."
  • He did not take questions but cast a vote Monday evening in favor of Matthew Byrne's nomination to be a district judge in Ohio. '
  • McConnell said he was ready to work on the farm bill, as well as on supporting NATO and Ukraine.

Driving the news: "Today, I'll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June," McConnell said in a Monday evening statement. "I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues."

  • He described his recovery as "a long and often frustrating process," noting "the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier."
  • McConnell added, "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me."

What to watch: Whether the Senate Agriculture Committee will set a hearing this week to finally move the farm bill forward with McConnell's help.

Catch up quick: McConnell, 84, was last seen at the Capitol on June 11. Since then, his team has provided few details about his health, fueling rampant online speculation.

  • McConnell said in July that he fell at his home in June, briefly lost consciousness and was treated for mild pneumonia after he was hospitalized.
  • The last official update came Aug. 6, when McConnell's office announced that he had been discharged from a rehabilitation facility and would continue recovering at home.
  • Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) and some prominent MAGA voices have pressed for more information and questioned whether McConnell remains fit to serve.

Friction point: The rumor mill kicked into overdrive in July, when Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) and former McConnell aide Scott Jennings made back-to-back statements saying they had substantive conversations with the hospitalized senator.

  • In a reported recording of an EMS call from the day of the senator's hospitalization, a dispatcher mentions cardiac arrest and a person receiving CPR at McConnell's address.
  • McConnell has had other health scares in the past, including freezing in front of reporters and prior falls. His office has pointed to the lingering effects of his childhood bout with polio.

State of play: McConnell is set to retire when his term ends in January.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect that McConnell voted Monday.

item.title: Trump and Jensen Huang unite against AI doomers in surprise on-stage call
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a surprise call from President Trump onstage at the All-In Summit Monday in Los Angeles, where the two dismissed fears of an AI takeover.

Why it matters: Trump and Huang are staking out an increasingly clear rejection of AI doomerism right as some of the world's most powerful CEOs and AI experts call for slower AI development over safety concerns.

Driving the news: Huang appeared to receive a call from Trump in the middle of an All-In Podcast interview Monday, according to video footage circulating on social media.

  • Huang put the president on speaker so the crowd could hear the conversation.

What they're saying: Trump and Huang shared an optimistic view of AI, highlighting its potential for economic growth and national security.

  • "The robots will not be taking over," Trump told Huang. "The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax," he said, referring to the recent wave of warnings about catastrophic AI risks.
  • Huang told Trump: "We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people."

Zoom out: Huang separately addressed the AI safety fears that erupted over the weekend, striking a more nuanced tone than Trump.

  • He said warnings from whistleblowers should be taken seriously, praising Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon for having "great courage" to raise his concerns about the company's AI development going too quickly.

Yes, but: Huang rejected predictions that AI could end the world as "not grounded in science."

  • He said AI companies should pause or pace their work "if they feel that their company is out of control."

The big picture: Huang has repeatedly dismissed AI doomer fears, suggesting that some cybersecurity alarm around AI can help drum up business for the security industry.

  • "What better way to create demand than to create a problem," Huang said at a Goldman Sachs conference in San Francisco last week, per Forbes. "Who doesn't want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?"

The bottom line: Nvidia has an enormous stake in the continued success of AI as a major supplier of the chips powering advanced AI models.

Go deeper: Here's how AI could kill us all (if the worst fears come true)
