item.title: Trump's USPS mail-ballot rules hit a second roadblock as Supreme Court weighs case
item.description:
A second federal judge blocked the U.S. Postal Service's new mail-ballot rules for the Nov. 3 midterms as the Supreme Court weighs whether to allow the restrictions in another case.

Why it matters: Sunday's order adds another hurdle to the Trump administration's bid to upend mail voting. The blocked rules would allow the USPS to refuse ballots that don't clear new standards, with mail voting already underway in some states.

The latest: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee in Washington, D.C., concluded Congress empowered the Postal Service to move mail, not to force states to enroll mail voters in a federal portal or to refuse ballots that fail its checks.

  • Nichols' ruling follows a similar order from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston blocking parts of the same rule. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals left Talwani's injunction in place on Sept. 10.
  • Talwani's order found the postal rules violate the U.S. Constitution and federal statute, while Nichols' new ruling relied entirely on his finding that Congress' Postal Reorganization Act doesn't allow many of the new rules.
  • The USPS did not immediately return requests for comment.

What they're saying: The White House wouldn't say if it planned to appeal this ruling but spokesperson Lauren Bis said election officials have had "ample time to prepare for the 2026 election."

  • Bis added in the emailed statement, "These are commonsense measures to protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans vote in American elections."
  • Kristen Clarke, NAACP general counsel, said in an email that two district courts and a federal circuit court have now blocked the Trump administration's "unlawful attempt to weaponize the U.S. Postal Service to hijack our mail voting system in the middle of an ongoing midterm election."
  • Clarke noted that the election is just 49 days away. "We urge the Supreme Court to reject this administration's request to green light this unlawful scheme and leave in place our mailing voting system which is safe, secure, and orderly," Clarke added.

Catch up quick: President Trump has long attacked mail voting, despite repeatedly using the method himself, including in August's Florida primaries.

  • His March executive order directed the Postal Service to develop new envelope, tracking and voter-list requirements for mail voting.
  • The Supreme Court already lifted an earlier injunction because the final rule hadn't been published yet. But after its publication, challengers returned to court and won new injunctions in Boston and D.C.
  • The Trump administration is now asking the high court to stop Talwani's order and allow the new rules.

Between the lines: Nichols said USPS might have the authority to issue rules on ballot-envelope designs, but he blocked the whole rule, finding its design, portal and rejection provisions too intertwined.

Friction point: Even with enforcement blocked, voluntary preparations have exposed how exacting the new system could be.

  • USPS initially rejected envelope designs from Florida's Leon County, a heavily Democratic area that includes Tallahassee, because the words "Return Service Requested" were 0.014 inches too close to other text, according to the Tallahassee Democrat.
  • An anonymous USPS whistleblower also told Congress the Postal Service's portal was rushed, and a single scanning error could cause a batch of ballots to be rejected.

The bottom line: The Supreme Court could rule on Talwani's injunction at any time. But Nichols' order now gives the administration a second injunction to overcome before it can enforce its mail ballot rules.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the White House and NAACP general counsel Kristen Clarke.

Catch up quick: President Trump has long attacked mail voting, despite repeatedly using the method himself, including in August's Florida primaries.

  • His March executive order directed the Postal Service to develop new envelope, tracking and voter-list requirements for mail voting.
  • The Supreme Court already lifted an earlier injunction because the final rule hadn't been published yet. But after its publication, challengers returned to court and won new injunctions in Boston and D.C.
  • The Trump administration is now asking the high court to stop Talwani's order and allow the new rules.

Between the lines: Nichols said USPS might have the authority to issue rules on ballot-envelope designs, but he blocked the whole rule, finding its design, portal and rejection provisions too intertwined.

Friction point: Even with enforcement blocked, voluntary preparations have exposed how exacting the new system could be.

  • USPS initially rejected envelope designs from Florida's Leon County, a heavily Democratic area that includes Tallahassee, because the words "Return Service Requested" were 0.014 inches too close to other text, according to the Tallahassee Democrat.
  • An anonymous USPS whistleblower also told Congress the Postal Service's portal was rushed, and a single scanning error could cause a batch of ballots to be rejected.

The bottom line: The Supreme Court could rule on Talwani's injunction at any time. But Nichols' order now gives the administration a second injunction to overcome before it can enforce its mail ballot rules.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the White House and NAACP general counsel Kristen Clarke.

item.title: Nationalist leaders say U.K. union "coming to an end"
item.description:
The first ministers of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales united Monday behind calls to leave the United Kingdom in an unprecedented alignment of nationalist leaders.

Why it matters: For the first time, all three first ministers favor leaving the U.K. — and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill says President Trump's support for a united Ireland has taken the debate global.

Driving the news: The nationalist leaders of the Scottish National Party, Sinn Féin and Plaid Cymru met in Cardiff, Wales, on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding declaring that the "political landscape across these islands is changing."

  • The SNP's John Swinney, Sinn Féin's O'Neill and Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth met as leaders of their respective parties, not as representatives of their regional governments.
  • Swinney and O'Neill called for referenda on independence from the U.K. during a news conference, but ap Iorwerth is pushing for similar regional powers as in Northern Ireland and Scotland and has ruled out holding a referendum during this term.

What they're saying: "For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end," the memo said.

  • "Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming," it added.
  • "We call for the British Government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction."

Zoom in: O'Neill told reporters that Trump's support for Irish reunification during a two-day visit over the weekend reflected a "growing conversation around constitutional change at home in Ireland."

  • She said the debate was happening "not just at home, but obviously now internationally as well" and Trump's intervention showed Irish unification is "very much on the table."

Yes, but: A spokesperson for U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Trump's comments don't change his stance that it's premature to call for independence referenda until public opinion clearly shifts.

  • The 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which largely ended decades of conflict in Northern Ireland, requires a referendum on Irish reunification if the British government believes a majority would support it.

The other side: Trump's comments drew backlash from British lawmakers and unionists, including Northern Ireland's Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly who criticized O'Neill's attendance at the summit in an interview with the BBC.

  • "She has not sought any agreement or permission from me to travel, attend or sign anything as first minister," the Democratic Unionist Party politician said.
  • Little-Pengelly stressed that she and O'Neill jointly lead Northern Ireland's power-sharing government and O'Neill was not there on official government business.

Go deeper: Why Trump's united Ireland stance hit such a nerve

item.title: Texas nominees' racist, vulgar remarks receive mixed GOP reaction
item.description:
Republicans have condemned, sidestepped or continued to support two Texas GOP nominees after one's racist post this weekend about students of color and another's years of vulgar comments about women sparked backlash.

The big picture: In a fiercely heated midterm election, some candidates' racist, sexist and crude material online hasn't always been enough to cost them their party's support.

  • Warning: This story includes crude, sexually explicit language that may disturb some readers.

Driving the news: House Speaker Mike Johnson was asked Sunday on CNN about vulgar comments Brandon Herrera, a YouTuber-turned-candidate running for a key Texas district, made online in the past — including calling a Nazi submachine gun the "original ghetto blaster."

  • In a 2023 clip played on CNN's "State of the Union" of Herrera addressing Moms Demand Action's Shannon Watts, he said, "Just because you let somebody cream-pie you doesn't mean I have to give a s--t about your political opinions. The fact that you kept your c-m trophy doesn't make you any less wrong about the dumb s--t that you say."
  • Johnson, who campaigned for Herrera, called the language "detestable" — but applauded his "very effective campaign." He continued, "That was — that was his [YouTuber] persona online, right? Right now, he's running as a very serious candidate for Congress and a very thoughtful guy."
  • Herrera is running for the seat ex-Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April after admitting to an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide. President Trump initially endorsed Gonzales but then threw his support behind Herrera.

Zoom out: Bo French, the Republican nominee for the state's Railroad Commission, which regulates the gas industry, sparked outrage this weekend after sharing a photo of students of color celebrating at a Texas Longhorns' game.

  • "I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," French wrote in the post that, at the time of this article's publication, had received some 36.7 million views.
  • In a separate post, he wrote that "social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners."

What they're saying: Sen. John Cornyn, who lost to a GOP challenger endorsed by President Trump, blasted the post, writing, "Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized."

  • Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), who did not have the president's support and lost to a primary challenger, also slammed French.
  • Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico praised Cornyn's condemnation and called on GOP nominee Ken Paxton to follow suit. Paxton didn't address French's post, instead directing his condemnation at Talarico as the one "dividing Texans by race."
  • Texas Gov. Greg Abbott stopped short of condemning French's post, though he said it was "not my message," and instead emphasized his support for freezing H-1B visas at universities.

Yes, but: It's not just Republicans with skeletons in their closets. Graham Platner's past social media posts dismissing sexual assault and denigrating police, plus his Nazi symbol tattoo, made him a ticking time bomb even before a rape allegation — which he denies — derailed his campaign.

  • But he rode out the earlier social media controversy for months, securing the party's nomination and key endorsements before ultimately suspending his campaign.

The bottom line: It comes in an era where more and more candidates' online lives and internet diatribes are becoming an un-erasable part of their record, haunting campaigns.

  • But in Herrera's and French's case, the Texas Republicans don't seem to be backing down from some of their comments that sparked the controversy. French has continued to double down even after fellow state Republicans have called on him to delete the post.
  • And in response to CNN reporting featuring his crude comments about women's weight, Herrera wrote last week, "Man, I forgot I was this funny."

Go deeper: Behind the Curtain: Trump's "caught on tape" women problem

item.title: Trump says a strong, smart president is the only "guardrail" AI needs
item.description:
President Trump lashed out at calls for new AI guardrails and protections on Monday, arguing AI only needs a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT" and that AI critics should "BEWARE!"

Why it matters: Trump continues to plant himself against calls for AI safety regulations as a growing chorus of AI leaders and CEOs, spearheaded by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei over the weekend, call for a slowdown in AI's development and better regulations to help keep humanity safe.

  • Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk agreed that AI is quickly becoming more powerful, potentially beyond what humans can understand and monitor, prompting calls for a slowdown.
  • The Trump administration has repeatedly clashed with Amodei and Anthropic, with the Pentagon previously designating the company as a supply-chain risk and stalling the release of its Mythos model.

What he's saying: Trump said Monday afternoon that fears of "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," putting it on par with Russian election interference claims and his own impeachments.

  • He said the AI development "will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces" under his presidency.

This was the second time he condemned AI safety fears in a 12-hour span. Early on Monday, he said that "the only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so."

Trump said his administration "has stopped AI 'people' from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,'" though he didn't elaborate. (The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment Monday.)

  • He also took a swipe at Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, "who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel.'"
  • "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!"
  • Trump also suggested there's "a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China."

Zoom out: Trump has continued to oppose tighter AI regulations, just as Washington is moving to discuss what can and should be done.

  • Trump, who has been pro-AI since his return to the White House, downplayed the need for AI safety checks and regulations on Sunday, suggesting to reporters that he didn't want to fall behind China in the race for stronger AI.
  • Trump's former AI czar David Sacks similarly pushed back against Altman and Amodei, saying the two can control AI's pace without a regulatory framework.

The other side: China's Foreign Ministry also criticized calls to slow AI development Monday, per CNBC.

  • "Fear-mongering, confrontation, competition will just disrupt [the] process of global AI governance," said Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: How Warsh can avoid a repeat of July's communications mess
item.description:
Seven weeks ago, Warsh took questions from the media, and it didn't go well. Markets sold off as he seemed vague and evasive about the reasoning behind the latest interest rate decision. Wednesday, he gets a do-over.

Why it matters: Investors will be thirsty for a more detailed explanation of the Fed's decision than the one Warsh offered in late July — even while respecting his intention not to give explicit guidance about future policy moves.

  • Markets are pricing in a quarter-point increase in rates — but the why behind that likely move is more significant than the act itself, for what it says about the Fed's analytical framework under its new leadership.
  • And if the Fed's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee elects to leave rates unchanged, Warsh will have an even trickier communications task, lest the bond market again start to question Warsh's willingness to use interest rate policy to keep inflation in check.

State of play: Assuming the Fed raises rates, does it reflect a belief that seemingly one-off changes to prices from tariffs and the energy shock are turning out to be more prolonged than previously thought?

  • Or is AI-fueled investment creating more sustained inflationary pressure? Is it simply that the neutral interest rate is higher than it seemed?
  • Not all interest rate adjustments are created equal. A "mid-cycle adjustment," like the three rate cuts enacted in 2019, or a "recalibration" or an "insurance move" imply different things from something like a "normalization" or a sustained policy tightening.

Between the lines: Of course, each of these potential answers has implications for what the Fed will do next, in tension with Warsh's deeply held desire to avoid anything resembling "forward guidance."

  • Moreover, different officials on the policy committee may have different rationales for a rate hike (or for not hiking), and as chairman Warsh has an obligation to accurately describe the range of views.
  • But there's a pick-your-poison dilemma he faces. If the Fed chairman fails to lay out a coherent framework and rationale for a policy move (or no move), people naturally start to wonder if there is one.

What they're saying: "We expect that he will frame the hike as a way to ensure that inflation returns to target in an acceptable timeframe," Christopher Hodge and Selin Aker at Natixis wrote in a note out this morning.

  • "We also think that he will emphasize that this decision was discrete and does not pre-commit the Fed to any actions in subsequent meetings, giving him and the Committee maximum flexibility to respond to shocks."

The bottom line: They teach us in the journalism business to ask the "who, what, when, where and why." At Wednesday's press conference, the first four will already be known.

  • Who = Kevin Warsh and the FOMC; what = an interest rate move or no move announced half an hour earlier; when = 2:30pm ET; where = the William McChesney Martin Jr. Building.
  • That leaves "why," which is the question that traders worldwide will be most eager to hear.

item.title: Washington's AI paralysis: Let 'er rip vs. hit the brakes
item.description:
President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain.

  • Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down.

Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress.

Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1, applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China.

  • Speaking in Ireland on Sunday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins."
  • It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or "pace the frontier" — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google.

Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations.

  • David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer: Slow yourselves down.
  • If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium.

  • Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand.
  • His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said Sunday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety.

The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency, but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet Tuesday to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority.

The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for.

  • On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison.
  • Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews.

What to watch: The unprecedented push for restraint from inside the AI industry, colliding with deepening public unease, could scramble this political stalemate.

  • Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a Trump ally running in a swing state, said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's new warning convinced him "we must slow down development" so government can catch up.
  • Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is investigating AI's "existential risk," while Sens. John Thune (R-S.D.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) are pursuing a narrower plan requiring companies to test and report catastrophic risks.

Reality check: Political pressure and lobbying could crack open the door to narrow bipartisan measures, though any meaningful regulation would still have to survive Trump's veto pen.

The bottom line: Washington is deeply divided on whether AI is a national triumph to unleash or a national emergency to contain.

  • Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand.
  • His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said Sunday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety.

The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency, but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet Tuesday to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority.

The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for.

  • On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison.
  • Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews.

What to watch: The unprecedented push for restraint from inside the AI industry, colliding with deepening public unease, could scramble this political stalemate.

  • Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a Trump ally running in a swing state, said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's new warning convinced him "we must slow down development" so government can catch up.
  • Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is investigating AI's "existential risk," while Sens. John Thune (R-S.D.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) are pursuing a narrower plan requiring companies to test and report catastrophic risks.

Reality check: Political pressure and lobbying could crack open the door to narrow bipartisan measures, though any meaningful regulation would still have to survive Trump's veto pen.

The bottom line: Washington is deeply divided on whether AI is a national triumph to unleash or a national emergency to contain.

item.title: How Republicans secretly got Fetterman for their convention
item.description:
The biggest surprise of last week's Republican midterm convention began with an audacious request from the organizers to GOP Sen. Dave McCormick: Could he get Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, a fellow Pennsylvanian, to make an appearance?

  • "I'll ask him," McCormick said. Within days, Fetterman — who's been increasingly at odds with the Democratic Party's liberal wing — was on board.

Why it matters: Fetterman's 64-second video — calling himself a "common-sense Democrat," praising McCormick and vowing to work with President Trump to defend Pennsylvania's steel industry — represented Fetterman's biggest break yet with his party.

Behind the scenes: According to three sources familiar with the talks, the idea for Fetterman to make the appearance emerged over the summer, as organizers of the Dallas convention sought what they called an "Oh sh*t" moment.

  • They were looking to drive home a key midterm message — that Democrats are too extreme.
  • Organizers discussed featuring "walk away" figures — people who had supported Democrats but had become disillusioned with the party.
  • Republican operative Tony Sayegh, a leading convention organizer, was a driving force behind the idea, and Trump adviser Jason Miller backed the plan. Fetterman topped their list.

Zoom in: Sayegh, a friend of McCormick's, took the idea to him in July.

  • McCormick had developed a friendship with Fetterman as the Democrat grew more estranged from his party, particularly over many Democrats' criticism of Israel.
  • Organizers knew getting Fetterman involved would be a massive coup.

The intrigue: McCormick approached Fetterman carefully, knowing the backlash his Democratic colleague could face if he agreed to a role in the GOP convention.

  • McCormick asked Fetterman to introduce him at the convention. A source said McCormick added: "I don't want you to do something that's not good for you."

The two senators hashed it out over calls and texts for a few days.

  • "I want to do it. I'm sure it will make people mad," Fetterman told McCormick, according to the source. "But you're my friend, and I want to introduce you."
  • Fetterman's decision was driven by his friendship with McCormick, not a desire to help Republicans, said a source familiar with his thinking. Fetterman "had no interest in being a pawn in a larger Republican play," the source said.

There was brief talk of Fetterman traveling to Dallas to introduce McCormick in person, but he decided against it.

  • Instead, Fetterman proposed recording a video outside a steel mill near his home in Braddock, Pa.
  • McCormick's team arranged for a videographer to meet him there.

Fetterman didn't use a script. He riffed in front of the camera.

  • He focused on introducing McCormick and highlighting their bipartisan work in support of Pennsylvania's steel industry.
  • Neither McCormick nor convention organizers tried to alter what he said. The notion of Fetterman switching parties never came up, according to a source familiar with the deliberations.

Organizers saw Fetterman's appearance as a jolt that would draw eyeballs to the first-of-its-kind midterm convention — and play big on social media.

  • To preserve the surprise, organizers kept the circle tight. McCormick looped in his chief of staff, Mark Isakowitz, and only a few others. Miller was Sayegh's point of contact in the White House.
  • Fetterman went even further: He told no one on his team, a source told Axios.

The bottom line: Fetterman's appearance at Trump's convention deepened his estrangement from the Democratic Party.

  • But Fetterman reiterated after his appearance that he isn't switching parties, calling himself a "lifelong Democrat" and saying that if Democrats win control of the Senate in November, he'd remain the "51st vote."

item.title: Dems' primary plan gives Native Americans more power
item.description:
The 2028 race for the White House will give new political clout to a long-overlooked constituency: Native American voters.

Driving the news: New Mexico now holds an influential early spot as one of the first states to vote in the Democratic primary — on Feb. 15, 2028. That's put Native Americans, who make up about 12% of the state, in position to wield more influence in the presidential race than ever before.

  • In recent Democratic primaries, New Mexico typically has voted late in the season, in June. States that held the earliest primaries had much smaller Native populations.
  • Now potential presidential campaigns are scrambling to adjust to the 2028 lineup, calling Native leaders to learn about Indigenous power players and the dynamics of tribal governments, Democratic operatives tell Axios.

Zoom in: Any presidential candidate who wants to win New Mexico is "going to have to listen to tribes," warned Deb Haaland, the former U.S. interior secretary who made history in 2021 when she became the first Native American to head a cabinet agency.

  • "We could be a large part in who that nominee is."
  • Native leaders and their allies say that will force presidential candidates to engage closely with tribal governments and pay attention to issues such as tribal sovereignty, land and water rights, and rural infrastructure.

Several potential 2028 contenders are already taking notes.

  • Isaac Dakota Casados, a New Mexico Democratic consultant and Navajo Nation member, told us his phone has been ringing off the hook as presidential campaigns-in-waiting look to learn more about Native voters.
  • "They're really trying to figure out how the Native American demographic plays into this larger picture," he said. "I think they're used to speaking to Hispanic and Latino populations within their states. This is a very unique variable that's very different to them."
  • Casados said Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker acknowledged to him that he's "really gotta learn" about tribal leadership, while New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker was "fascinated" by New Mexico's myriad tribal cultures in a recent conversation.
  • Kalyn Free, a Choctaw Nation citizen who's on the Democratic National Committee's powerful rules and bylaws committee, also said she's been getting outreach from presidential hopefuls and their teams.

The jockeying among 2028ers to win Native American voters could help elevate new power brokers in the Indigenous community.

  • Tribal governments will likely be courted for endorsements. Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, is uniquely poised to become a sought-after validator for 2028 candidates in Indian country: She's running for governor of New Mexico this year.
  • Some potential 2028 contenders already appear to be wooing Haaland. She met recently with Booker and is rallying with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg this weekend. Pritzker helped raise money for Haaland at an event in New Mexico this month.
  • Haaland told us she talked with Pritzker about her efforts to investigate the troubled legacy of federal Indian boarding schools and President Trump's slashing of protections for Native American sacred sites.
  • Asked if she would endorse a candidate in the 2028 primary, Haaland said: "I would wait to see."

Zoom out: New Mexico has the nation's third-largest share of people who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native, and it includes 23 federally recognized tribes.

  • When New Mexico votes in the presidential primary, the race will probably have been narrowed to two or three candidates — giving the state an oversized say in helping pick the party's nominee, Democratic strategists say.

Native leaders say their community's voters don't easily map onto the party's progressive-vs.-moderate divide, and stressed that the community isn't a monolith in general elections, either.

  • In the 2016 Democratic primary, Hillary Clinton won some states with significant Native populations, such as New Mexico and Arizona — but Bernie Sanders carried others, such as Alaska and Montana.
  • In 2024's general election, some Native voters across the country — who polls suggested had been hit particularly hard by inflation — shifted toward Trump.

What's next: Democrats hope that by putting New Mexico early in the primary lineup, they'll learn how to better win Native Americans and reverse that trend.

  • "These votes really matter," said New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D), noting that Native voters have been the margin of difference for presidential candidates in some battlegrounds. "We credit the Navajo Nation vote to getting Biden over the finish line in Arizona" in 2020.

Flashback: This year Native American leaders lobbied the Democratic National Committee to add New Mexico to the early primary calendar.

  • In February, the All Pueblo Council of Governors passed a resolution that said doing so would "transform the relationship between presidential candidates and Pueblo peoples," whereas the old lineup had been "effectively silencing" Native voices.

Axios' Russell Contreras contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump's $5,000 checks require Congress to approve, Johnson says
item.description:
President Trump's proposal to send adult U.S. citizens $5,000 dividend checks would require congressional approval, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said on Sunday.

Why it matters: Trump and his top officials claim they can send the checks without Congress — even with the prospect of them costing upward of $1.3 trillion.

What they're saying: "He'd need Congress to act," Johnson said in a CNN interview.

  • Johnson told George Stephanopoulos on ABC's "This Week": "The question is, how do you pay for it? How do you be able to pass the legislation to put more money back in the pockets of hard-working Americans? That's the objective. We should all be wanting to do that, to put the issue of affordability front and center and ease the burden on Americans."
  • Asked by NBC's ""Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else."

Driving the news: President Trump, at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas, said this week he'd order a $5,000 check — a "Trump Dividend" — if Republicans retained control of the House and the Senate.

  • Trump and other officials have said the dividend would be funded by tariffs, gains on investments and other income.
  • The president told reporters before departing Ireland on Sunday that "the $5,000 checks are going forward" and that he had thought of this plan "a while ago."
  • When a reporter asked why not do the checks now instead of after the midterm elections, given Republicans currently control Congress, Trump replied: "Because if the Democrats get in, our country will be in shambles."

The big picture: Such a massive stimulus also comes with significant economic risks, both to the deficit and inflation.

  • The idea has already met bipartisan opposition, though Trump has insisted the offer and the checks will happen.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details throughout.

item.title: Why Trump's united Ireland stance hit such a nerve
item.description:
President Trump stood by his support for a united Ireland on Sunday after his remarks during a two-day visit sparked a backlash from unionist and British politicians and praise from Irish nationalists.

Why it matters: Trump broke with a longstanding U.S. presidential convention of not taking sides on whether Northern Ireland should ultimately be British or Irish.

  • The U.S. helped broker the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, built around consent and parity between British unionism and Irish nationalism.
  • Former President Clinton, whose administration played a central role in the peace process, explicitly said the U.S. was "neither in favor of a united Ireland nor opposed to the idea."

Driving the news: Trump said in Dublin, sitting beside Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin on Saturday, that he'd "love to see" Ireland unified and that it is "going to happen eventually," so it "may as well happen now."

  • He described uniting Northern Ireland with the Republic of Ireland as "fantastic," adding: "The U.K. would have something to say about it obviously, but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?"
  • Trump later said Irish reunification would be a "very cool thing" while noting that "no matter what you say or how you say it, there's no good answer."

On Sunday, Trump told reporters: "It just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland. It seems to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together."

  • He added this was only his opinion, but "many people agree" and he "had so much support" in response to his remarks.

Between the lines: Trump has managed the unusual feat of delighting Irish nationalists while alarming some Northern Irish politicians who have previously expressed support for him.

  • Martin revealed that Trump has privately expressed the same preference before.

What they're saying: While Irish nationalist politicians seized on Trump's comments and said "the conversation on Irish unity has shifted," unionists in Northern Ireland and politicians in Westminster swiftly condemned the remarks.

  • Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, who represents East Belfast in Parliament, said on X, "Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington. Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people."
  • Robert Jenrick from Nigel Farage's Reform Party said on X that Trump was "completely wrong," adding: "Northern Ireland is, and will always be, a proud part of the United Kingdom."

A 10 Downing Street spokesperson said in a media statement that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's position on Irish unification remains unchanged from previous comments he's made that a referendum on a united Ireland was "off the table" as he's "not aware ​that there is majority public support" for one.

  • The spokesperson added that Burnham is committed to upholding the Good Friday Agreement, which largely ended three decades of conflict known as the Troubles, established Northern Ireland's current system of government and largely removed visible signs of the border.

Context: Under the Good Friday Agreement, Northern Ireland remains part of the U.K. unless voters in Northern Ireland choose reunification and voters in Ireland approve the constitutional change — putting democratic consent, rather than the preference of London, Dublin or Washington, at the center of its constitutional future.

Flashback: It's not the first time that Trump has floated the idea of a united Ireland.

  • In March, he joked about a Northern Ireland-Republic "merger" in Washington.

item.title: Johnson calls for AI solutions but says Congress won't take the lead
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday that Congress won't lead the charge on regulating AI safety.

Why it matters: Calls for AI companies to adopt safety protocols reached a fever pitch this week, prompting the four biggest AI labs to endorse slowing their models' development.

Driving the news: Johnson was urged this week to cancel the House recess and bring representatives back to D.C. to pass a law on AI safeguards.

  • During a Sunday appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," Johnson said Congress intervening isn't the answer and that AI companies can halt their work at any time.
  • We have to "resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium. It's got to be done right, safely, wisely.

In a separate appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press," Johnson conceded that he would recall House members and schedule a vote on AI regulation "if we had a solution," but said any action from Congress must be done carefully.

  • "We have to put up some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn't run away ....But at the same time, we've got to make sure that we don't lose our edge in the global competition on this with China. Because that would be a national security threat."

What they're saying: Johnson told CNN and NBC he would like to organize a meeting between President Trump, members of Congress, and the top AI officials who call the shots at their respective companies.

  • Johnson added to CNN that he would prefer AI company leaders to take a leadership role and responsibility for ensuring the safety of their products, rather than pushing Congress to implement rules.
  • Johnson's comments mirror former White House AI czar David Sacks, who said late Saturday that the major labs should simply pace development on their own, without the government having to intervene.

The other side: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told ABC's "This Week" that Democrats planned to meet Tuesday morning to discuss AI.

  • "We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, slow down the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," he said.

Zoom out: CNN's Jake Tapper pointed out that several AI leaders agreed with a 3,800-word essay published Saturday by Anthropic's Dario Amodei, in which he proposed slowing AI development and implementing more safety measures.

  • Johnson seemed skeptical, saying that the companies "all have very different ideas on what the guardrails should be. There's no consensus among them. And Congress is obviously less qualified than the people who are pushing this frontier to know all the ins and outs of it."
  • The House speaker also said Americans shouldn't panic over the technology and the doomsday warnings, though Axios' Andrew Solender reported last week that rank-and-file members of Congress are urging action.
  • "We need to handle this new technology like we have others in the past and make sure we're doing everything we can responsibly to also not smother American innovation. We have to do both things simultaneously," Johnson said.

Go deeper: Labs are begging for someone to slow the AI race

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from additional comments to NBC and comment from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries
item.content:encoded:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday that Congress won't lead the charge on regulating AI safety.

Why it matters: Calls for AI companies to adopt safety protocols reached a fever pitch this week, prompting the four biggest AI labs to endorse slowing their models' development.

Driving the news: Johnson was urged this week to cancel the House recess and bring representatives back to D.C. to pass a law on AI safeguards.

  • During a Sunday appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," Johnson said Congress intervening isn't the answer and that AI companies can halt their work at any time.
  • We have to "resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium. It's got to be done right, safely, wisely.

In a separate appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press," Johnson conceded that he would recall House members and schedule a vote on AI regulation "if we had a solution," but said any action from Congress must be done carefully.

  • "We have to put up some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn't run away ....But at the same time, we've got to make sure that we don't lose our edge in the global competition on this with China. Because that would be a national security threat."

What they're saying: Johnson told CNN and NBC he would like to organize a meeting between President Trump, members of Congress, and the top AI officials who call the shots at their respective companies.

  • Johnson added to CNN that he would prefer AI company leaders to take a leadership role and responsibility for ensuring the safety of their products, rather than pushing Congress to implement rules.
  • Johnson's comments mirror former White House AI czar David Sacks, who said late Saturday that the major labs should simply pace development on their own, without the government having to intervene.

The other side: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told ABC's "This Week" that Democrats planned to meet Tuesday morning to discuss AI.

  • "We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, slow down the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," he said.

Zoom out: CNN's Jake Tapper pointed out that several AI leaders agreed with a 3,800-word essay published Saturday by Anthropic's Dario Amodei, in which he proposed slowing AI development and implementing more safety measures.

  • Johnson seemed skeptical, saying that the companies "all have very different ideas on what the guardrails should be. There's no consensus among them. And Congress is obviously less qualified than the people who are pushing this frontier to know all the ins and outs of it."
  • The House speaker also said Americans shouldn't panic over the technology and the doomsday warnings, though Axios' Andrew Solender reported last week that rank-and-file members of Congress are urging action.
  • "We need to handle this new technology like we have others in the past and make sure we're doing everything we can responsibly to also not smother American innovation. We have to do both things simultaneously," Johnson said.

Go deeper: Labs are begging for someone to slow the AI race

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from additional comments to NBC and comment from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries

item.title: AI's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes
item.description:
In nine startling hours on Saturday, the four biggest AI labs — which rarely agree on anything — set aside years of feuds and competition to endorse a slower development pace for their models.

  • Their new stance: Prioritize safety over growth, even at a cost.

The big picture: AI's unrelenting growth has hit an inflection point with the public, Washington and even the companies building it.

  • Data centers are unpopular. People are panicked about doom scenarios. And 51 days before midterms, legislators suddenly realize there are points to be won by cracking down.

Against that backdrop, the industry's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes Saturday.

  1. At 10 a.m. ET, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei dropped a 3,800-word essay saying model development needs to be paced, otherwise doom scenarios are possible — like a rogue-agent takeover of the entire internet, which he said could be as soon as six months from now.
  2. An hour later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shocked the AI chattering class by quoting Amodei's essay on X and saying "Dario is right." Musk — who heads SpaceXAI, formerly xAI — had pointedly not joined previous industry-wide calls for any kind of slowdown.
  3. At 12:30 p.m., OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tweeted: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier." In an interview Friday that was released on Saturday, Altman told Fortune his company won't go public this year, dashing hopes for a blockbuster IPO. He said OpenAI has too much safety work to do and would be better off doing that as a private company.
  4. At 7 p.m., Demis Hassabis — the Nobel laureate who co-founded and chairs Google DeepMind, and is Alphabet's chief scientist — tweeted: "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward. The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment."

Between the lines: Publicly putting safety ahead of technological or financial growth may be the industry's only route to avoid a crackdown that's not on its terms.

  • Legislators are begging House Speaker Mike Johnson to stay in session and do something about the "threat" of AI.
  • The more extreme alternative is something like Sen. Bernie Sanders' push to force a pause and make the most advanced AI illegal.

Reality check: Most people realize there's too much money at stake to just stop moving forward. But the tradeoff may be between historic riches and slightly less historic riches.

  • Let's see whether they actually agree on what oversight ("embedded third-party evaluators") and "slow" mean, then follow through.

Friction point: No one in China is having the same kind of we'd-better-stop moment.

  • Influential Silicon Valley tech voices, including former Trump official David Sacks, spent Saturday highlighting the counterargument that slowing down just lets adversaries — with no such safety qualms — catch up. In a late Saturday-night post, Sacks effectively dared OpenAI and Anthropic to voluntarily pace the AI frontier without waiting for the government. "If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop."
  • Amodei even acknowledged that a safety regime only really works if authoritarian governments come to the table, too. "Pacing within democracies will be limited by the lead that U.S. companies have over authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party," he wrote. "If we slow down by more than this amount, then (unpaced) CCP-associated projects will pull ahead, creating significant national security risk."

The bottom line: Saturday may go down as the day AI changed — when industry moguls vowed to limit themselves.

  • Read Amodei's essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier."

item.title: The tab is coming due for America's borrowing binge
item.description:
Americans are facing a rising tab as a multi-decade borrowing binge collides with a spike in energy prices caused by the Iran war.

The big picture: Long-term interest rates are surging, as are consumer prices.

  • It's a toxic mix of near-term inflation pressures and years of fiscal imbalance.

Driving the news: The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note rose to 4.97% Friday, up a full percentage point since the end of February, and only a hair below its high since 2007.

  • The rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has risen in lockstep, reaching 7.08% Friday, per Mortgage News Daily — the highest in more than a year.

State of play: The immediate catalyst Friday was an inflation report that showed consumer prices surging higher in August, with gasoline prices accounting for more than a third of the gain.

  • Gasoline is now at a national average of $4.29 a gallon, while the price of diesel has climbed to over $6 a gallon.

All this means that the Federal Reserve is now expected to raise its target interest rate this week.

  • But longer-term borrowing rates are set in global markets — and determined by bigger forces.
  • The U.S. government is spending about $2 trillion a year more than it raises in taxes at a time the cumulative debt is already roughly 100% of a year's GDP.
  • Long-term bond yields have been rising worldwide, reflecting both high government borrowing and demand for capital from the AI buildout.

The intrigue: The recent spikes have taken place in spite of interventions by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to try to smooth turbulent bond markets — efforts that haven't succeeded in making borrowing cheaper.

  • And rather than focus on the deficit reduction the bond market wants, President Trump has floated the notion of $5,000 payments to all U.S. adult citizens if Republicans win midterm elections.
  • The U.S. government is already spending around $1 trillion a year in interest on the debt, on track to rise to $2 trillion over the next decade, a new high as a share of the economy. If the recent surge in rates is sustained, those numbers will grow even higher.

The bottom line: The combination of near-term energy-driven inflation and the long-term debt trajectory means that it will cost more to borrow money for the foreseeable future.

item.title: OpenAI delaying IPO amid AI safety concerns, Sam Altman says
item.description:
OpenAI will not go public this year given all the safety work it needs to do, CEO Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview released Saturday.

Why it matters: Altman's comments come as fears over doomsday AI scenarios have ramped up since an Anthropic employee resigned and issued a dire warning about AI's capabilities.

What they're saying: "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," Altman said.

  • "I would say not 2026, yeah. We got a lot of stuff to do," Altman told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell.
  • "Meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together, I'm happy to be able to do that as a private company."

The intrigue: The market expected blockbuster IPOs from both OpenAI and Anthropic this year.

  • Altman's move puts the ball squarely in Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's court — especially given Amodei's warning Saturday that AI development needs to be slowed.

The bottom line: "I think a key principle that we should all agree on is that we cannot take actions that would risk losing control of the future to AI," Altman said.

  • That means investors may have to wait a while.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with new information throughout.

item.title: Anthropic, OpenAI CEOs call for slowdown in AI development
item.description:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling for an immediate slowdown in the pace of AI development, warning of potentially devastating consequences in a matter of months otherwise.

  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly agreed that the industry needs to slow the pace of frontier-model advances and take more steps on safety.

Why it matters: Amodei pulled no punches in a new essay, cautioning that swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet in as little as six months from now.

The big picture: This is the week that the AI safety debate broke into the public consciousness, driven by an Anthropic employee's very public resignation and warning of possible doom.

  • Amodei's essay isn't necessarily a direct response, but it will have much the same effect amid a sudden surge of public and congressional outrage.

What they're saying: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote.

  • "The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try."

Threat level: He also specifically referenced the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face rogue agent incident, which he said could have been far worse.

  • "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails," he warned.

Zoom out: Amodei said Anthropic would unilaterally take one key safety measure — giving external evaluators employee-level access to ensure safety procedures and report incidents.

  • He called on the rest of the industry to do the same.
  • He also called for coordination among democratic countries to establish safety standards, and an effort for those countries to coordinate with authoritarian governments as well.

Zoom in: Anthropic executives followed Amodei's essay with a call for legislative and regulatory responses.

  • "The government has a critical role to play here, including blocking the sale of the most advanced chips to adversarial nations like China, enacting a national law requiring testing of frontier models, with the power to block the most advanced models that prove to be unsafe," public policy chief Sarah Heck wrote on X.

The intrigue: SpaceXAI's Elon Musk quickly endorsed Amodei's call to action.

  • "Dario is right," he wrote on X. (Anthropic is a major customer of Musk's for data center capacity.)
  • OpenAI's Altman later posted that "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," and said his company would also give access to external evaluators.

Reality check: So much money is at stake in the AI industry that it can be hard to imagine companies restraining themselves, especially if they're not sure competitors will do the same.

  • Just last month, OpenAI said it would slow development of its newest model, Astra, due to cybersecurity concerns.
  • Anthropic itself has gone back and forth on the value of unilaterally slowing development.

In fact, Amodei's critics suggested the essay was as much about market position as safety.

  • "Dario makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic," venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya wrote on X.

The bottom line: Amodei's essay is likely to have a significant impact on the safety and regulatory debate.

  • But whether anyone acts, or if the industry simply continues hurtling toward an incredibly uncertain future, remains to be seen.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional context throughout.

item.title: Anthropic report: 5 ways Claude was exploited for war, spying and repression
item.description:
The AI safety debate exploded this week over warnings that the technology could one day destroy humanity.

  • Anthropic's latest threat report offers a more immediate wake-up call: Today's models are already helping U.S. adversaries develop kamikaze drones, hunt dissidents and conduct dangerous virus research.

Why it matters: AI is tearing down barriers that have long constrained the world's most dangerous actors. A handful of people can now mount operations that once required legions of spies, engineers or hackers.

Driving the news: Anthropic — the safety-focused lab behind Claude — says it spent the past eight months tracking and disrupting attempts to misuse its models. Among the most alarming cases it uncovered:

1. An Iran-linked operation used Claude to help target U.S. naval forces.

  • Claude helped build targeting handbooks tracking ship positions, U.S. personnel, aircraft and ship identifiers, satellite imagery and websites exposing naval movements.
  • Other Iran-linked operations tapped the model for propaganda, domestic surveillance and targeting opposition figures and minorities.

2. Claude served as an engineer for a Yemeni team building missiles.

  • A weapons cell in northern Yemen relied on Claude Code to develop guidance software for rockets and missiles.
  • The team had separate copies write code, conduct research and check one another's work. After one guided-rocket test apparently failed, they returned to Claude within hours to diagnose what went wrong.

3. A China-linked operation used Claude to hunt Uyghurs.

  • Anthropic says the actor sifted through more than 100 WhatsApp groups and dozens of Telegram channels to identify Uyghurs in Syria who could be pressured or paid to report on armed Uyghur groups.
  • Claude then helped a non-Arabic-speaking operator carry out covert outreach in Syrian Arabic — translating replies and coaching efforts to exploit money problems, family separation and relatives still in Xinjiang.

4. One man used Claude to help build surveillance for 25 million phones.

  • A consultant in Mali relied on Claude as the main engineering force behind a nationwide system capable of collecting call records, texts and voice traffic.
  • The system could identify people by voice across different SIM cards, flag VPN users and generate intelligence dossiers on any phone number without a warrant.

5. Claude refused dangerous virus research — so the request went to another AI.

  • Researchers on a state-backed grant were trying to alter chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus, to spread more easily or evade immune defenses. The work was intended for a military research institute.
  • Claude blocked the most sensitive requests, so the platform routed them to a rival model with weaker safeguards — a stark reminder that one lab's safety rules only go so far.

Between the lines: Frontier AI labs are becoming unlikely intelligence agencies in their own right.

  • The same models that empower bad actors can also give their makers an early window into malign activity — like Anthropic's discovery of Russian drones designed to select human targets without human approval.
  • That could give frontier labs an extraordinary view of emerging threats, even as AI allows ragtag groups, lone operators and other hard-to-track actors to mount far more sophisticated attacks.

The big picture: This week has lit a fire under Washington, with lawmakers suddenly treating AI safety as an urgent political issue.

  • A bipartisan group of House lawmakers is urging Speaker Mike Johnson to cancel recess until Congress acts, while Sen. Bernie Sanders — perhaps the most outspoken AI critic in Congress — wants to ban superintelligence outright.
  • Still, sweeping federal AI safety rules remain elusive, particularly with President Trump dismissing extinction fears Friday and framing the greater danger as losing the AI race to China.

item.title: Behind the Curtain: It's not too late
item.description:
The White House, Congress and the country's leading AI companies have allowed AI to grow faster, stronger, more powerful and wildly lucrative (and dangerous), with no serious effort to control it or spread the benefits beyond the super-wealthy.

  • It's not too late to change this. But if they all dither, duck or dance around it, the chances of AI worst-case scenarios will explode, likely early next year, according to almost every person we talk to privately who truly understands AI.

Why it matters: The technology is getting better, faster than anyone envisioned — with the possibility rising that AI will self-improve and do wildly unpredictable things.

  • The good news: There's now a growing public cry for attention and action and, at least in private, a broad understanding of what could be done relatively fast with bipartisan and industry buy-in.

The big picture: In July, I wrote an essay for The Wall Street Journal saying America "faces one of those rare, historic moments when government, business, schools and families could be working together to meet a truly generational challenge: winning the AI race. So far, we're blowing it."

  • Two short months later, the technology is vastly better — and the societal response vastly dumber. As a nation, we're choosing to amuse or distract ourselves.

Here's how to change that fast, based on our months of conversations with lawmakers, White House officials and AI labs. Think of what follows as me channeling their private views:

  1. Sound an all-hands-on-deck alarm. Every political topic is trivial and small compared to AI. We will look back in shame if we get spooled up about trans bans or $5,000 checks when countless AI insiders are warning of catastrophic outcomes. Let's say they're all paranoid and delusional. If so, it still doesn't matter: we've never seen this much investment in one technology this fast in human history. It's seeping into every industry and every job and every community and every screen, at a speed never before witnessed by man. Yes, we need a special session of Congress and select committees. But we need even more: AI execs, bioterror specialists, job-training wizards and safety experts convening to plan for scenarios and act fast.
  2. An AI governing body with teeth and speed, ASAP. This isn't rocket science. Most major labs want this and would agree to it, as long as it applies to all rivals and competitors. This body would need the expertise to understand these models, and the power to review and shut them down if they display dangerous behavior. It can't operate at typical regulatory speed — it needs to move as fast as the technology. It's nonsense to think you can't advance AI development fast and regulate it wisely simultaneously.
  3. A universal standard for data centers to benefit communities and taxpayers. The top AI companies would take this deal in a heartbeat: They get to build and operate data centers provided they supply a community's energy, offset water use or environmental damage, transparently report on their building and business plans, and spread the financial benefits to local residents. These execs are spooked by the public backlash and ready to aggressively spread the financial benefits, with dividends or cash. So make them.
  4. Engage China. We shouldn't trust them, and they shouldn't trust us. But trust me: the only way to ultimately control AI on a worldwide scale in coming years will be for the two superpowers to create some kind of framework modeled after how we've safely governed nuclear weapons for decades. We need to start this discussion now so potential collaboration is possible in the coming years. To those who think China will never consider this seriously: Are you sure an authoritarian regime really wants AI once it hits recursive self-learning and can't be controlled by anyone, including an autocratic regime? We're winning the AI race now, and may never have more leverage to shape this joint effort.
  5. Build coordinating infrastructure. What I wrote in the WSJ is even more needed today: "Bring together the best and brightest drawn from the federal government, from the leading AI companies, from business and labor, from economics, from public health, from ethics to form a working group with actual authority. People who are paid to anticipate, not to react haphazardly." This group would have four primary functions: map potential problems and upsides before they hit, build the (policy) playbooks before they're needed, level with the American people along the way, and expedite work to deliver widespread AI benefits.

Reality check: Yes, President Trump opposes regulation or bipartisan efforts. Yes, AI companies are obsessed with more money, more speed. But the politics are shifting fast: If you listen closely to Vice President Vance, you can hear rising worry. At this pace, toxic AI politics could force mind-changing that was unthinkable two months ago.

item.title: The world reconsiders America
item.description:
America is shedding its status as the default choice for foreign governments to park money, buy weapons and send students.

Why it matters: Even modest shifts away from the U.S. could chip away at advantages that have helped sustain American economic and geopolitical power for decades.

Driving the news: The Netherlands moved 86 tons of gold out of the U.S. and Canada last week, citing the move as a hedge against "extreme systemic risks." France already moved all of its gold out of New York, while Germany debated doing the same.

  • Norway's sovereign wealth fund — the world's largest — announced plans to reduce its holdings of U.S. government bonds amid turbulence in the Treasury market.

The big picture: Beyond finance, European countries are looking for ways to wean off the U.S.

  • On weapons, Europe is seeking to source more equipment locally to reduce its dependence on American firepower, Reuters reports.
  • On technology, the EU this summer set out plans to reduce its reliance on American companies, drafting cloud rules that would restrict Amazon, Google and Microsoft from competing for sensitive contracts, Reuters also reported.

Zoom out: Individuals around the world are also recalibrating their relationship to the U.S.

  • International applications to U.S. colleges dropped 10% in the most recent admissions cycle. Stricter international student visa policies and the Trump administration's broader immigration posture have weighed heavily.
  • International travel to the U.S. fell 5.5% in 2025, the first decline since the pandemic, as relationships with longtime allies grew strained. Canadian travel dropped 25% last year, with the slide continuing into early 2026.
  • German travel to the U.S. has dropped 25% since the beginning of Trump's term, with the country's travel association pointing to politics as one factor.

By the numbers: America's standing has been hit especially hard in the West, according to a recent Pew study.

  • Hungary and Poland were the only two of 10 countries polled where majorities still view the U.S. as a reliable partner.
  • Majorities in all 10, including two with right-wing populist leaders, say they lack confidence in Trump to do the right thing in world affairs.

Reality check: This is not wholesale abandonment of U.S. partnership. The U.S. dollar's dominance remains unthreatened, allies depend heavily on American military might and the U.S. remains the top destination for international students.

What to watch: Germany, Italy and Spain are facing renewed pushes at home over whether to keep gold reserves in the U.S.

item.title: Jewish institutions' security spending tops $1 billion as antisemitism persists
item.description:
Antisemitic threats have pushed the nationwide cost of protecting Jewish synagogues, schools and community centers past $1 billion a year, new estimates reveal as congregations prepare for big crowds during the High Holy Days, which began Friday with Rosh Hashanah.

Why it matters: Enhanced security has become a growing expense for Jewish communities, congregation leaders say, often taking up money that could pay for teachers, summer camps, elder care and other programs.

By the numbers: Jewish communal institutions are now spending an estimated $1.02 billion annually on security, a record high, according to new data from the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA).

  • That's up 33% from the federation's previous annual estimate of $765 million in 2024.
  • More than 4,500 synagogues, Jewish community centers, schools, summer camps and other nonprofits spend an average of roughly $225,000 each, the group said.
  • Security personnel — including guards and security directors — account for the largest share.

Of that total, about $150 million goes toward security technology and the "hardening" of buildings — upgrades that can include security cameras, reinforced doors and controlled-entry systems — as well as maintaining existing security equipment.

  • The estimate doesn't include security costs at more than 1,600 kosher restaurants, about 500 kosher markets and groceries, and other privately owned Jewish businesses.

State of play: Synagogues are increasingly moving beyond security guards and cameras to layered, year-round systems that include hardened entrances, trained congregants as security personnel and coordination with police.

  • More than 7,100 volunteers now help protect more than 500 synagogues and events each week, according to Community Security Service (CSS), a nonprofit that now protects more than 500 synagogues across the U.S.
  • The expanded security comes as assaults linked to antisemitism have reached their highest level since the Anti-Defamation League began tracking them in 1979.

What they're saying: "I cannot tell you whether we're safer or less safe," CSS CEO Richard Priem told Axios. "I can tell you that there's a lot more capability right now protecting the Jewish community than there was a few years ago."

  • JFNA CEO Eric Fingerhut said the tradeoff is stark. "Every dollar our community spends on guards and cameras is a dollar not spent on Jewish education."

Context: The estimated Jewish communal security tab is more than three times the size of the entire federal grant pool available to vulnerable nonprofits nationwide.

  • FEMA made $300 million available through the FY 2026 Nonprofit Security Grant Program for nonprofits at high risk of terrorist or extremist attacks.
  • A bipartisan bill introduced in Congress this year, the Jewish American Security Act, would authorize $1 billion annually from FY 2027 through FY 2031 for the grant program, and loosen limits on using the money for security personnel.

Yes, but: More recent data present a mixed picture. Antisemitic incidents surged after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, rising 140% that year and climbing again to a record high in 2024, according to the Anti-Defamation League.

  • FBI data show reported anti-Jewish hate crime incidents fell 21% in 2025, from 1,938 to 1,528, but were still the third-most on record.
  • Anti-Jewish incidents still accounted for about 63% of all religion-based hate crimes and 14% of all reported hate crimes last year.
  • Separately, the ADL found overall antisemitic incidents fell 33% last year, even as physical assaults rose to a 46-year high.

item.title: Record diesel prices stoke food inflation, transportation costs
item.description:
The record price of diesel threatens to stoke inflation at a time when consumers are already price-sensitive and businesses are reeling from higher costs due to trade tensions.

Why it matters: Diesel is a key cost throughout the supply chain, meaning soaring prices could eventually show up in what consumers pay for everything from groceries to household goods.

Driving the news: The national average price of a gallon of diesel topped $6 for the first time ever, AAA said Friday, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reports.

  • That's up 60% from a year earlier.

Between the lines: Food prices could be among the first places consumers feel the ripple effects, executives said this week.

  • At grocery chain Kroger, which has been trying to keep a lid on prices: "I would expect that the pressure is actually going to mount," CEO Greg Foran said Friday on an earnings call.
  • At pork producer Smithfield Foods: "That impact is beginning to flow through in the second half of the year," CFO Mark Hall said Thursday.
  • At Hormel Foods: "With the Iran war and the spike in diesel costs, that's been something we've had to confront," interim CEO Jeffrey Ettinger said Wednesday.

But the effects extend well beyond food.

  • For example, at Newell Brands — whose portfolio includes Rubbermaid, Sharpie and Coleman — the inflationary impacts of energy costs have far exceeded the company's initial estimates.
  • "It's either resin, which is obviously dependent on the price of oil, or it is direct transportation costs, i.e., diesel," CFO Mark Erceg said Tuesday.

The big picture: Energy prices have spiked since President Trump launched the war with Iran, which prompted the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping lane.

  • The latest Energy Information Administration outlook expects retail diesel to average $4.40 a gallon in 2027, up 33 cents, or 8.2%, from its previous forecast of $4.07, Axios' Rebecca Falconer and Ben Geman reported.
  • The average price of unleaded gasoline has also spiked, rising by $1.11 over the last year to $4.30 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA.

By the numbers: 47 of the 50 states have experienced an increase in average diesel prices of more than $2 per gallon over the last year, according to GasBuddy analyst Patrick De Haan.

  • The economy is facing an extra $300 million in diesel costs every 24 hours.
  • California is poised to become the first state with average diesel prices above $8 — with many stations already above $9, according to GasBuddy.

The bottom line: Record diesel prices are turning the energy shock into a broader cost shock for businesses and consumers.
