item.title: Trump bans some Canadian imports as North America trade war intensifies
item.description:
President Trump said the U.S. would ban Canadian alcohol, some dairy products and large motorcycles, sharply escalating a trade war largely fought with tariffs.

Why it matters: The measures deepen the economic rift between countries that have spent decades interlinking commerce, threatening disruption for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border.

Zoom in: The import bans take effect Sept. 29, effectively cutting off U.S. market access for the targeted Canadian goods rather than simply making them more expensive.

  • Trump imposed the bans under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to bar imports from countries that maintain or increase discrimination against U.S. commerce.
  • The White House said on Tuesday it would also expand the existing 50% tariffs to dozens of additional Canadian products — including some steel and aluminum goods, furniture and paper — effective Sept. 15.

What they're saying: A senior administration official played down the potential economic fallout, noting that the measures target products where Canada has little U.S. market share or buyers can turn to domestic and other foreign suppliers.

  • The administration removed a handful of products from the list of goods subject to 50% tariffs — including cement, road salt and certain hospital paper products.
  • The official said the administration adjusted the tariff list based on feedback from businesses, removing some products where officials found U.S. supply chains were particularly dependent on Canadian imports.

Catch up quick: Trade tensions have ratcheted up swiftly since U.S.-Canada talks collapsed last month.

  • The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods. Canada hit back with tariffs of up to 50% on a similar amount of U.S. goods, a measure that took effect earlier Tuesday.
  • Trump has since threatened higher tariffs on Canadian autos starting next year.
  • On Monday, he also threatened to ban Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier from selling its jets in the U.S. (Such a measure is not in the proclamations announced today, with a senior official saying it is still under consideration).
  • In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, Trump said he would direct officials to shut Canadian-made products out of a broad range of U.S. government contracts, "unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies."

Zoom out: Canada's restrictions on American alcohol have been a particular source of frustration for U.S. officials.

  • Most provinces have kept U.S. booze off government-run liquor store shelves for much of the trade war.

What to watch: The two economies are so deeply intertwined that escalating trade tensions could run into political and economic limits.

  • Unlike many of Trump's earlier tariffs on Canada, the Section 338 measures do not spare USMCA-compliant goods, leaving more of the countries' integrated supply chains exposed.
  • Canada initially included U.S. lobster in its retaliatory tariffs, only to soon change course amid concerns that the tariffs would be too painful for Canadian businesses.
  • In the U.S., Trump's threat to ban Bombardier jets quickly got the attention of Republican Sen. Jerry Moran, who warned of the potential impact on Kansas workers.

Go deeper: Trump's next trade weapon

item.title: Trump's summer of sabotage
item.description:
Congressional Republicans are preparing to share the stage with a president who has spent the August recess complicating their efforts to run their races on their own terms.

Why it matters: Republican lawmakers fled Washington for the latter part of the summer, eager to localize their races.

  • But President Trump keeps nationalizing the election.
  • In the process, he's staking out positions that run counter to GOP orthodoxy on issues including beef imports and child care subsidies.

Driving the news: The Trump administration's plan to extend federal child care subsidies to families with a stay-at-home parent is the latest policy flashpoint.

  • His call to rename New Mexico is his most recent cultural one.
  • The child care proposal — championed by Vice President Vance — sparked backlash from some conservative lawmakers and pundits who tagged the policy as "socialism" at a time when Republicans have made anti-socialism a central campaign message.
  • And whatever the merits of calling New Mexico "New America," it's likely not what Greg Cunningham, the GOP candidate in NM-03, will focus on when he takes the stage at the convention.

Between the lines: Although Trump isn't formally taking attendance at the convention, there will be some notable absences.

  • Sen. Susan Collins won't make it — and isn't making an excuse. Sen. Dan Sullivan will stay home to prepare for a Saturday debate.
  • More than 100 GOP lawmakers are expected to skip the event.

Zoom out: Trump has repeatedly forced Republicans to grapple with policies that aggravate their constituencies or collide with their own ideological convictions.

  • His plan to import up to 300,000 metric tons of beef tariff-free for 90 days inflamed GOP lawmakers in red states.
  • More than a dozen GOP senators publicly criticized the move, warning it would hurt American cattle ranchers.

Imposing higher tariffs on Canadian goods threatened to bring a trade war to two must-win border states: Maine and Michigan.

  • And his call Monday to target Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier could have outsized economic implications in Kansas, a red state with an increasingly competitive Senate race.
  • Trump ally Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) was forced to break with Trump over the call to boycott. Bombardier is a key employer in Kansas.

Republicans are taking an à la carte approach to data centers, which have suddenly become a political liability. Candidates in both parties have been scrambling to distance themselves from the industry.

  • But Trump isn't brooking any nuance on the issue, calling communities that oppose data centers "backwards and poor." He doubled down four days later.

Trump reacted to a surprisingly strong jobs report Friday by threatening to cut off trade with certain countries unless the Federal Reserve lowered interest rates.

  • Congressional Republicans spent months defending the Fed's independence amid the administration's attacks on then-chair Jerome Powell — even leading to a hold-up on the confirmation of Trump's chosen new Fed chair.
  • Trump seems to be wading back into the interest rates fight as inflation and affordability become the GOP's biggest election concerns.

Trump is also restarting hostilities with Iran, dashing any GOP hopes that gas prices will drop before November.

The bottom line: With less than two months to go until Election Day, Trump's coattails are increasingly looking short or nonexistent — and this week's midterm convention could either reverse or entrench that trend.
item.content:encoded:
Congressional Republicans are preparing to share the stage with a president who has spent the August recess complicating their efforts to run their races on their own terms.

Why it matters: Republican lawmakers fled Washington for the latter part of the summer, eager to localize their races.

  • But President Trump keeps nationalizing the election.
  • In the process, he's staking out positions that run counter to GOP orthodoxy on issues including beef imports and child care subsidies.

Driving the news: The Trump administration's plan to extend federal child care subsidies to families with a stay-at-home parent is the latest policy flashpoint.

  • His call to rename New Mexico is his most recent cultural one.
  • The child care proposal — championed by Vice President Vance — sparked backlash from some conservative lawmakers and pundits who tagged the policy as "socialism" at a time when Republicans have made anti-socialism a central campaign message.
  • And whatever the merits of calling New Mexico "New America," it's likely not what Greg Cunningham, the GOP candidate in NM-03, will focus on when he takes the stage at the convention.

Between the lines: Although Trump isn't formally taking attendance at the convention, there will be some notable absences.

  • Sen. Susan Collins won't make it — and isn't making an excuse. Sen. Dan Sullivan will stay home to prepare for a Saturday debate.
  • More than 100 GOP lawmakers are expected to skip the event.

Zoom out: Trump has repeatedly forced Republicans to grapple with policies that aggravate their constituencies or collide with their own ideological convictions.

  • His plan to import up to 300,000 metric tons of beef tariff-free for 90 days inflamed GOP lawmakers in red states.
  • More than a dozen GOP senators publicly criticized the move, warning it would hurt American cattle ranchers.

Imposing higher tariffs on Canadian goods threatened to bring a trade war to two must-win border states: Maine and Michigan.

item.title: Historic NYT v. OpenAI copyright battle heats up
item.description:
A landmark copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 moved into a critical new phase Friday, as all three parties presented their official arguments to a judge, with hopes of a favorable ruling ahead of a possible trial.

Why it matters: A ruling in favor of the Times could wreak havoc on the lucrative business models underpinning the AI industry.

  • A ruling in favor of OpenAI and Microsoft would serve as a massive blow to the publishing industry, potentially undermining its ability to control and monetize how content is scraped and used by AI giants.

Zoom in: In its motion for summary judgment, the Times argued OpenAI and Microsoft copied its works at scale to build commercial substitutes, which it believes violates the law.

  • OpenAI argued existing copyright laws and legal precedents allow tech giants to scrape publicly available works to train their large language models, and that reported facts are not protected by copyright law.
  • It cited studies that suggest outputs to queries via ChatGPT do not create commercial substitutes of the Times' work. Microsoft made similar claims for its Copilot AI product.

How it works: In its filing, OpenAI cites two recent California federal court decisions, Kadrey v. Meta and Bartz v. Anthropic, which found using copyrighted works to train AI models constituted as "fair use" in both of those cases because the training was considered transformative.

  • The Times disputes that the AI training was transformative, and also says those cases are different and can't be applied to this suit because those plaintiffs didn't show that AI outputs competed with their products, creating market substitutions for their journalism.
  • The Times also argues that the case, which it filed in a New York federal court, should be evaluated against binding copyright precedents established by higher courts — the Supreme Court and the Second Circuit — rather than those recent lower court rulings.

Zoom out: Around the world, the case is being closely watched as a groundbreaking legal precedent that could shape the future of the AI industry.

  • This is especially true for the Trump administration, which has publicly tied its national security and economic goals to the development of AI infrastructure.
  • On Thursday, the Justice Department filed a brief supporting OpenAI in the case, arguing training large language models from millions of digital works delivers a transformative public benefit that offsets any competitive harm to the publishing industry.

What to watch: District Judge Sidney Stein is expected to rule in the coming months whether the case, or key portions of it, should move to trial next year.

Disclosure: Axios has a content licensing and technology agreement with OpenAI, focused mostly on expanding our local coverage. Go deeper.

Editor's note: This article has been corrected to more accurately reflect the Times' viewpoint on the prior court decisions that OpenAI is citing for their defense.

item.title: Why House Republicans are pulling their $5 million from a key N.Y. battleground seat
item.description:
House Republicans are effectively abandoning what was supposed to be a key battleground district in New York over concerns that their candidate, state Sen. Peter Oberacker, is too flawed to seriously compete, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: Expect to see more of this cold calculus as the general election heats up, with both parties determining where their money will actually make enough of a difference to be worth spending.

  • In this case, the GOP has determined that New York's 19th district, a perennial battleground seat that has routinely changed hands between Democrats and Republicans over the last several election cycles, doesn't warrant the investment.
  • The seat, currently held by freshman Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.), was one of the National Republican Congressional Committee's stated targets as recently as last month.

Driving the news: Congressional Leadership Fund, House Republicans' main super PAC, removed all its money in the district last week, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact.

  • The group had $4.8 million in television ad reservations supporting Oberacker, all of which were pulled on Friday.
  • The NRCC also removed Oberacker from its "MAGA Majority" list, according to Punchbowl News.
  • The NRCC and CLF did not provide comments on the record for this story.

Between the lines: Oberacker is seen by Republicans on Capitol Hill as too flawed a candidate to seriously challenge Riley, according to multiple GOP sources familiar with the matter.

  • One major issue that sources cited is the controversy around a post Oberacker made on Facebook in 2015 praising his grandfather's military service in Nazi Germany.
  • Another is his campaign's cash burn rate: He had raised around $1.2 million as of the end of June but spent nearly $850,000 of it, including $350,000 on consultants, according to campaign finance filings.
  • The Oberacker campaign's spending, one source told Axios, has been a source of behind-the-scenes tension with national Republicans.

What we're hearing: "Spending a few million in Upstate New York against Riley — who, ... it's not like he's got a lot of enemies, and he raises money — it's just a hard environment, hard to argue," a Republican source told Axios.

  • Oberacker's "internals have him down ... and then there's the Nazi thing, which is not a killer, but when you add them all up it's like, 'eh,'" the source said.
  • A House Republican told Axios that "those who know New York know the Lawler, Suozzi, and Gillen races were the only ones ever actually considered competitive," referring to swing-district Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) and Laura Gillen (D-N.Y.).
  • The Oberacker campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection
item.description:
LIV Golf — the Saudi-backed league that upended the sport with a costly splash but failed to identify a viable business model — filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on Tuesday.

Why it matters: It's an ignominious turn of events for a brash organization that lured some of the biggest stars away from the PGA Tour with enormous paydays that proved to be unsustainable.

The big picture: LIV represents a high-profile flop for its Saudi investors.

  • The bankruptcy filing comes after months of efforts to lure new backers and chart a new path for a league that struggled to draw significant TV ratings.

Catch up quick: The Public Investment Fund — Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund — confirmed in April that it was withdrawing support for the league after the 2026 season.

  • PIF — which ultimately plunged more than $5 billion into LIV, according to Money in Sport — decided to ditch LIV after President Trump's war in Iran scrambled geopolitics in the Middle East and jolted energy prices.
  • The fund said in a statement that the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term is no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

Between the lines: LIV said Tuesday that it had secured a restructuring support agreement from an arm of BC Partners to reorganize operations and emerge "majority owned by players."

  • The bankruptcy could lead to the severing of key contracts, including with star players like Jon Rahm, whose defection to LIV was considered a significant loss for the PGA Tour.
  • It could also serve as a major turning point in the career of superstar Bryson DeChambeau, one of the initial players to leave the PGA for LIV.
  • PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp has made it clear that any players who want to return will need to earn their way back, calling the tour a meritocracy by its nature.
  • LIV said Tuesday that it "remains in advanced discussions with" the players.

Friction point: Critics of LIV and the players who joined it said the league amounted to "sportswashing" as the Saudis sought to redirect attention from human rights abuses.

  • Defenders — including LIV member and former PGA superstar Phil Mickelson — said the league would help grow the game on a global scale.

item.title: AI agents are poised to be the next hacking victims, cyber CEO predicts
item.description:
In a world of AI-enabled cyberattacks, the victims of hacks will no longer just be humans — they'll also be AI agents themselves, Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios.

Why it matters: Cyber defenses are tailored toward predicting and defending humans. Now, companies need to start treating the agents roaming their systems as both potential adversaries and the targets.

Driving the news: Gerry's prediction during an interview at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last month came after OpenAI disclosed that its agentic system hacked Hugging Face but before the AI lab released its technical deep dive into how its agents carried out that attack.

What he's saying: "We're going to see agents as the victim," Gerry told Axios. "You're going to start to see agents getting hacked, not people."

The big picture: Gerry's prediction comes as AI labs continue to grapple with the long-tail impact of their agents taking unauthorized actions during pre-deployment security testing.

  • But many of those cases involve AI agents acting in unintended ways, not hacking each other as a way to break into an organization.

Zoom in: Gerry fully anticipates that the growing number of hacks against AI agents are going to take place in the enterprise, rather than on consumer-owned and operated agents, since that's where the bulk of AI agents are currently deployed.

  • "It's going to become the No. 1 attack vector that we're going to see," he said. "To make our lives easier as humans, we've given [AI agents] the crown jewels to everything."
  • He noted that many tools that companies have long relied on now also have agents themselves, making it harder to keep track of what's on a company network.
  • "You have all of these enterprise-approved tools that now magically got AI turned on," he said. "Now, there's a backlog of all of this tech debt of things that I approved that I no longer approve."

Between the lines: The cybersecurity industry has been trying to raise awareness about securing AI agents' identities for more than a year, warning that AI agents are now the latest example of insider threats.

  • Those insider agents could be leveraged to provide hackers with unfettered access to sensitive systems, exfiltrate data and break into other parts of an organization.
  • "To me, that's inevitable," Gerry said.

Zoom out: Even before AI agents started to proliferate in enterprise networks, poor identity controls were one of the top vectors for malicious hackers.

  • Identity-based cyberattacks accounted for 60% of all of Cisco's incident response cases in 2024, for example.

The intrigue: Visibility of the actions that AI agents are taking and their chain of thought is becoming more obfuscated as frontier models advance, making it more difficult for security teams to attribute attacks.

What we're watching: "It's new attacks. It's moving faster. It's moving at a bigger scale," Gerry said.

  • "But ultimately, this comes back to good cyber hygiene and understanding what exists and how do you put controls around it."

Go deeper: AI models are becoming unknowable

item.title: Smithsonian chief to retire after clashes with White House
item.description:
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced he will retire later this year following clashes with the White House.

Why it matters: Bunch's departure leaves the Smithsonian facing a leadership transition as the Trump administration escalates efforts to reshape how the institution presents American history.

Driving the news: Bunch will step down by the end of the year after nearly 38 years at the Smithsonian, the institution said Tuesday.

  • "It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation," the 73-year-old said.

Flashback: Bunch pushed back against a White House review of the Smithsonian in a July message to staff, saying the report was "not a fair characterization" of the National Museum of American History.

  • He said the Smithsonian remained committed to "scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy, and integrity."

Zoom out: Bunch was the Smithsonian's first Black leader and earlier founded the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

  • During his tenure, Congress authorized two new Smithsonian museums: the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum and the National Museum of the American Latino.

What's next: The Smithsonian's Board of Regents will name an acting secretary and launch a national search for Bunch's successor.

Go deeper: Why Trump's Smithsonian museums culture war worries historians

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: Trump's next trade weapon
item.description:
Trump is reaching for a more drastic trade war weapon, with new threats to shut foreign goods out of the U.S. altogether.

Why it matters: It would mark a significant evolution of the administration's trade agenda, with potentially bigger economic fallout than the tariffs that have defined it so far.

  • Trump may also have firmer legal footing for some import bans than emergency tariffs. Federal trade laws explicitly give presidents the power to prohibit imports under certain conditions, even where courts have rejected their authority to impose tariffs.
  • Businesses can absorb the cost of a tariff, pass it on to customers, or some combination of both. But losing access to a key part or product altogether can result in shortages, stalled production and a chaotic scramble to find new suppliers.

Driving the news: Trump threatened to ban Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier from selling jets in the U.S., just hours before Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods took effect this morning.

  • "NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.'"
  • The Bombardier threat came days after Trump responded to the strong jobs report with a social media post demanding that the Federal Reserve lower interest rates, tying the demand to a sweeping threat to cut off trade with nations that would in theory include countries like Canada, Japan and China.
  • "LOWER THE RATE OR I'LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT," Trump wrote. Notably, he added: "IT'S BETTER THAN TARIFFS!"

Between the lines: Top Trump trade official Jamieson Greer has also floated outright bans, saying last month that it could be an option to hit back at Canada's retaliatory tariffs.

  • "We've never done these bans; it's quite extreme. But maybe we need to," Greer said in an interview with the CBC late last month.
  • Greer also said in July that Trump "for sure can" use emergency powers to restrict trade, after the president threatened to cut off trade with Spain.
  • At the time, Greer pointed to the Supreme Court's ruling that blocked Trump's emergency tariffs, noting that law "clearly says you can prohibit trade."

The intrigue: The U.S. has banned imports before, though usually as part of sanctions against adversaries rather than as leverage in a trade dispute with a close economic partner like Canada.

The Supreme Court ruling that blocked Trump's emergency tariffs highlighted that a more potent option was available to him.

  • The Court ruled that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs, but the law explicitly allows presidents to prohibit imports. Trump seized on that distinction the day the ruling came down. "I can embargo, but I can't charge one dollar," he told reporters.
  • Justice Brett Kavanaugh called that an "odd donut hole" in oral arguments, noting that a president could shut down trade entirely, but couldn't impose even a 1% tariff.
  • Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which Trump has already invoked against Canada, also allows the president to exclude a country's goods under certain conditions.

What to watch: Trump's Bombardier threat is already showing the political realities that can complicate such drastic trade moves.

  • The company — and the firms that supply it — are deeply embedded in the U.S. economy, particularly in Kansas. It employs over 1,000 people in Wichita and buys from roughly 2,800 U.S. suppliers across 47 states.
  • Kansas Republicans were quick to hint at the potential for economic fallout of an outright import ban.
  • "I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas," Sen. Jerry Moran posted on X.
item.content:encoded:
Trump is reaching for a more drastic trade war weapon, with new threats to shut foreign goods out of the U.S. altogether.

Why it matters: It would mark a significant evolution of the administration's trade agenda, with potentially bigger economic fallout than the tariffs that have defined it so far.

  • Trump may also have firmer legal footing for some import bans than emergency tariffs. Federal trade laws explicitly give presidents the power to prohibit imports under certain conditions, even where courts have rejected their authority to impose tariffs.
  • Businesses can absorb the cost of a tariff, pass it on to customers, or some combination of both. But losing access to a key part or product altogether can result in shortages, stalled production and a chaotic scramble to find new suppliers.

Driving the news: Trump threatened to ban Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier from selling jets in the U.S., just hours before Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods took effect this morning.

  • "NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.'"
  • The Bombardier threat came days after Trump responded to the strong jobs report with a social media post demanding that the Federal Reserve lower interest rates, tying the demand to a sweeping threat to cut off trade with nations that would in theory include countries like Canada, Japan and China.
  • "LOWER THE RATE OR I'LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT," Trump wrote. Notably, he added: "IT'S BETTER THAN TARIFFS!"

Between the lines: Top Trump trade official Jamieson Greer has also floated outright bans, saying last month that it could be an option to hit back at Canada's retaliatory tariffs.

  • "We've never done these bans; it's quite extreme. But maybe we need to," Greer said in an interview with the CBC late last month.
  • Greer also said in July that Trump "for sure can" use emergency powers to restrict trade, after the president threatened to cut off trade with Spain.
  • At the time, Greer pointed to the Supreme Court's ruling that blocked Trump's emergency tariffs, noting that law "clearly says you can prohibit trade."

The intrigue: The U.S. has banned imports before, though usually as part of sanctions against adversaries rather than as leverage in a trade dispute with a close economic partner like Canada.

The Supreme Court ruling that blocked Trump's emergency tariffs highlighted that a more potent option was available to him.

  • The Court ruled that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs, but the law explicitly allows presidents to prohibit imports. Trump seized on that distinction the day the ruling came down. "I can embargo, but I can't charge one dollar," he told reporters.
  • Justice Brett Kavanaugh called that an "odd donut hole" in oral arguments, noting that a president could shut down trade entirely, but couldn't impose even a 1% tariff.
  • Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which Trump has already invoked against Canada, also allows the president to exclude a country's goods under certain conditions.

What to watch: Trump's Bombardier threat is already showing the political realities that can complicate such drastic trade moves.

  • The company — and the firms that supply it — are deeply embedded in the U.S. economy, particularly in Kansas. It employs over 1,000 people in Wichita and buys from roughly 2,800 U.S. suppliers across 47 states.
  • Kansas Republicans were quick to hint at the potential for economic fallout of an outright import ban.
  • "I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas," Sen. Jerry Moran posted on X.

item.title: OpenAI's historic math solution overshadowed by credit controversy
item.description:
OpenAI says its AI has solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem, a potentially historic breakthrough shadowed by questions over unpublished research by outside mathematicians.

Why it matters: The controversy strikes at a core trust question for AI-assisted science: whether researchers can safely use frontier labs' tools to work on unpublished discoveries.

State of play: OpenAI said Tuesday an internal model "significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra" produced a proof that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations can develop a singularity in finite time.

  • The company says the effort began Sept. 1, after OpenAI researchers heard rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been solved and launched its new internal model at the remaining problems.
  • On a call with reporters, OpenAI executives said they devoted enormous computing power to the effort, putting the cost of solving the problem in the "millions of dollars" with roughly 10,000 agents at work.
  • The equations help explain how fluids move, which could be used to better understand everything from blood circulation to weather patterns.

Friction point: NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge had been working on closely related fluid-dynamics research.

  • Buckmaster publicly questioned whether OpenAI raced down a research direction it learned about from their work and raised concerns about whether private Codex material could have played a role.
  • He also alleged that OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck pushed to remove Alpöge from authorship because he works for Anthropic, OpenAI's biggest competitor.
  • Buckmaster said that when he threatened to make their interactions public, Bubeck allegedly responded: "Why would you ruin your career?"

Between the lines: The controversy raises thorny questions about who owns the work completed with AI tools, and whether the labs are competing with their own customers.

Zoom in: OpenAI says it did not access Buckmaster or Alpöge's specific user data while pursuing the proof. But the company acknowledged Tuesday that it can't entirely rule out an indirect connection.

  • "While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models," OpenAI said.
  • By default, OpenAI says it doesn't train on inputs or outputs from enterprise customers. Users of personal ChatGPT accounts can opt out of having their conversations used for training.

What they're saying: "Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X.

  • Altman admitted OpenAI launched the effort after hearing rumors that Anthropic's models had solved a major math problem: "We were curious if ours could do it too."
  • OpenAI says it does not intend to claim the $1 million Millennium Prize, instead framing the result as evidence of how quickly its most advanced systems are improving.

Mady's thought bubble: It's striking that OpenAI spent millions of dollars in compute chasing a math breakthrough after hearing that outside researchers — including an Anthropic employee — were close to one themselves.

  • The episode raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the company providing scientists with AI research tools can also mobilize vastly more resources to compete with them?

The bottom line: Disputes over what AI companies know about your work and usage of their tools are just beginning.

item.title: NYC unveils records suggesting officials knew air was unsafe after 9/11
item.description:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration released more than 170,000 pages of documents Tuesday that suggest city officials knew air conditions following the 9/11 attacks were unsafe, despite assurances otherwise.

The big picture: Twenty-five years later, New Yorkers are still seeking a full accounting of what city officials knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero and whether they were honest with the public about the risks.

  • More New York City Fire Department members have died of 9/11-related illnesses than the 343 killed in the attacks.
  • "It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way, and yet we know that could not be further from what actually happened," Mamdani said during Tuesday remarks.
  • "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air."

Driving the news: The release includes air quality reports, contamination records and internal correspondence that shed light on what city officials knew about the toxic air near Ground Zero.

  • The public portal where the memos are stored was a more than $34 million commitment from City Hall, Mamdani said.
  • The released followed a settlement struck between Mamdani's administration and advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which has waged a long fight for transparency.

9/11 Health Watch executive director Ben Chevat said Tuesday that "since 9/11, four different mayoral administrations worked to keep the answer from the public, even as city officials at the time continued to say that the air was quote 'safe and acceptable.'"

  • The portal hosts what was found in 68 boxes of toxin-related documents uncovered by City Hall officials last year and archives from former Mayor Rudy Giuliani's office, like the so-called Harding Memo that predicted lawsuits related to toxic exposure, among other records.
  • Mamdani said that the city would continue to update the portal and, as part of the settlement, would appoint designated personnel to coordinate document gathering to help individuals obtain victim health benefits.
  • Since its 2011 reopening, the federally funded 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund has awarded more than $16.8 billion to over 71,000 claimants, per its most recent annual report.

Flashback: Christine Todd Whitman, the former head of the Environmental Protection Agency under the Bush administration, told The Guardian 10 years ago that she was wrong to assure New Yorkers that the air was safe.

What they're saying: Comedian Jon Stewart, who in the years following the attack became a vocal advocate for first responders' health, said at Tuesday's announcement that the city "buried" evidence for 25 years, starting soon after the attacks.

  • He put it bluntly: "The city began covering their ass three weeks in."

Go deeper: Accused 9/11 plotters to stand trial in 2028

item.title: The body image battle is real in 2026, but the bodies may not be
item.description:
A societal spotlight on extreme thinness is stripping body diversity from screens, just as fashion magazines did in the early aughts, mental health experts tell Axios.

The big picture: Fake content creators are introducing unattainable, AI-generated body images that prey on human nature and exacerbate the struggle for many to reach self-acceptance for their bodies.

  • When shrunken celebrities "become the ideal ... because of their status, then the virtual influencers are going to be emulating that," Katy Bruchmann, who leads Santa Clara University's Social Cognition and Comparison Lab, says.
  • "Then, the more really thin, super beautiful virtual influencers you have, the target changes for all the real people again. It's a really scary cycle."

Driving the news: Some are posing as influencers selling wellness products or services, while others are sharing body transitions or beauty advice.

  • Axios reviewed dozens of social media posts that include clear AI-generated body transformations or fitness influencers, while online sleuths have uncovered content that appears fake.

Zoom in: Some were labeled as AI. Many were not. But research from Brooke Bennett, the director of the Body image, Eating, Access, and Media Lab at the University of Clemson, and her colleagues found that it essentially doesn't matter.

  • Even when people know the image they're viewing is AI, it still hurts their body satisfaction.
  • "I think it's this expectation management piece," Bennett says. "We might... say, 'OK, I know that person's AI, but that doesn't mean that everyone else knows, and people are going to expect me to look like that too.'"

Zoom out: The striving for thinness has been fueled by a GLP-1 boom and pushed to extremes with dangerous internet trends. While "SkinnyTok" was banned by TikTok, the messages are still slipping through.

  • Coupled with images of flawless women wearing a size 00, social media can be a body image minefield.
  • "In the clinical space, we're seeing patients coming in really struggling to deal with some of this AI and ... social media pressures in general," Bennett says.

Follow the money: Tech and media companies have flooded the zone with a host of cyber stars that are accessible and low-cost.

  • "You can hire an AI influencer for cheap, and they can be in Brazil tonight selling a beverage, and in Tokyo tomorrow selling a T-shirt," Bruchmann says.

Our thought bubble: Beyond the completely virtual vixens, it's easier than ever to edit images using AI.

  • I tried it myself, asking ChatGPT to slim me down. I still looked like myself, with no immediate signs that the photo had been altered, like garbled text or extra fingers.

The fine print: When organic AI content is posted to Meta products, users can opt in to identify it, or Meta's system may.

  • TikTok "encourage[s]" creators to label content generated or significantly edited by AI. The platform may also label it.
  • But the rules aren't foolproof, and likely AI-generated content still appears unlabeled.

Reality check: Zoë Bisbing, founding director of Body-Positive Therapy NYC, tells Axios that body diversity (yes, real bodies) is still online.

  • "It's true — the thin ideal is getting thinner," she says. "At the same time, it's not hard to find size diversity on the street, at the beach and [in] your algorithm."
  • Start simple by searching terms like body acceptance, body positive or body liberation, she says.

Go deeper: TikTok glorifies weight loss among teens, young adults: Study

item.title: Sports' grip on America sparks summer of political warfare
item.description:
The WNBA, Major League Baseball and even a golf startup spent the summer as unlikely proxies in some of the country's fiercest national conflicts.

Why it matters: American culture has shattered into thousands of tiny shards of glass. But sports remains one of the few forces powerful enough to pull much of the country into the same moment — making it a prime target for political fights.

  • That kind of shared attention has become a scarce and ultra-valuable resource for activists, politicians and companies.

Zoom in: This summer's fights have blown up far beyond the fan bases involved.

  1. Caitlin Clark, the WNBA's biggest star, spent the season absorbing hard fouls. The fight over whether refs were protecting her quickly became a fight about race. Eleven House Republicans wrote to the league and the topic has become a staple on conservative media.
  2. Clark's Indiana Fever teammate Sophie Cunningham told ESPN in July that girls shouldn't have to compete against "biological men." Competing activist groups have clashed outside WNBA games, with Cunningham's words and photos appearing on signs held by her supporters.
  3. Three San Francisco Giants pitchers wrote Bible verses on their rainbow caps for Pride Night in June. The Justice Department referred the league to the EEOC for possible religious discrimination after it warned the players about violating uniform rules.
  4. Good Good Golf, a popular YouTube channel and apparel brand, posted an ad last month showing its co-founder shoving a female golfer to the ground. Callaway responded to the uproar over the video by ending a three-year partnership, and Good Good withdrew as the title sponsor of a new PGA Tour event. As commercial consequences for Good Good piled up, conservative commentators took up the cause as an example of cancel culture overreach.
  5. President Trump's shadow hung over this summer's World Cup. His threats to pull matches from Democratic-led cities and his close alliance with FIFA president Gianni Infantino — who presided over the reversal of a U.S. player's suspension before a critical game — prompted global backlash against FIFA for letting one politician shape the sport.

By the numbers: The NFL alone accounted for 83 of last year's 100 most-watched telecasts in the U.S. College football added seven. Two World Series games, the Kentucky Derby, the men's NCAA basketball final and a boxing match pushed the sports total to 95.

  • The remaining five were President Trump's address to Congress, his inauguration, former President Biden's farewell speech, the Oscars and the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Between the lines: The WNBA is the clearest example. It's one of the fastest-growing major sports leagues, filling arenas and becoming a national cultural force in just a few years.

  • A game between Caitlin Clark's Indiana Fever and the Chicago Sky last month averaged 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock — the most-watched regular-season game since the league's opening weekend in 1997.
  • But the league's biggest stories increasingly happen off the court, where players' personalities and opinions can generate attention faster than games.
  • Substacker Derek Thompson called it a "derivatives market" of sports commentary, where most of the conversation is about the conversation rather than the basketball.
  • He noted that Fox News published stories about Cunningham's comments six times in one day.

Reality check: America has long fought some of its biggest cultural battles through sports: Muhammad Ali refused to join the Army after being drafted during the Vietnam War and Colin Kaepernick knelt during the national anthem.

The bottom line: As long as sports hold the country's attention, it will keep drawing political fights.

item.title: 2026 candidates target health care "corruption"
item.description:
Campaigning on health care used to mean talking about coverage or costs. Now, in the run-up to the midterms, it's just as likely to focus on "corruption."

The big picture: Candidates are accusing primary or general election opponents of being in the pockets of drugmakers, insurers and other powerful health interests, to the detriment of voters.

  • It's a strategy that plays into affordability concerns and voter anger at the health system — but frequently avoids addressing what about the system needs fixing.
  • "Voters want leaders to lower everyday costs and firmly believe that will require taking on political corruption, corporate power and special interests' influence," public opinion firm Lake Research Partners wrote last month in a survey of attitudes about affordability and accountability.

Zoom in: That thinking is influencing the tone of one of the most competitive House races in the country, in Iowa's 1st Congressional District. GOP Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democrat Christina Bohannan, along with their surrogates, have accused each other of caving to big health insurers and undermining patient care.

  • In Michigan, Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed called his Republican opponent Mike Rogers a "pharma lobbyist," prompting Rogers' campaign to send a cease-and-desist letter and threaten legal action.
  • Charges of coziness with health industries also are surfacing in key Senate races in New Hampshire and Nebraska.
  • And some democratic socialists have played up drug and insurer donations to incumbents in primary challenges, as was the case when Melat Kiros knocked off 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado's 1st Congressional District.

Between the lines: Polling shows medical costs are the public's top economic worry.

  • Democratic challengers are trying to leverage that sentiment by focusing attention on opponents' campaign contributions, while Republicans tend to key on Democratic policies they say are handouts to certain industries.
  • The Lake Research Partners survey, commissioned by the progressive PAC Indivisible Action, found voters respond to the idea that rising costs stem primarily from corporate greed, corrupt CEOs and price gouging instead of government spending and waste.
  • "Voters aren't just concerned about the economy today; they are fed up with the resulting unfairness of a rigged system," it stated. "They see insiders, politicians, and corporations with too much power and elected leaders prioritizing their interests while ordinary people pay the cost."

Flashback: GOP lawmakers in Congress and outside conservative groups portrayed the Affordable Care Act as a profit-making machine for health insurers last year as they rallied to allow the expiration of pandemic-era enhanced subsidies.

  • A recent NPR analysis of YouTube ads found Republican candidates are now trying to get ahead of criticism of the subsidy expiration, and of health spending cuts in last year's sweeping reconciliation bill, by focusing on fraud in Medicaid, rural hospitals and affordability.
  • But Democrats think they can pin more health care cost issues on Republicans — and are highlighting policies in the reconciliation bill they say upended millions of lives and widened gaps in care.
  • Some are also criticizing President Trump's drug pricing deals, saying they really delivered big pharmaceutical companies tax breaks, regulatory relief and other perks.

What's next: House Democrats have already vowed to reverse the Medicaid cuts in the reconciliation bill and restore the enhanced ACA subsidies. But there's an added oversight component some are talking up on the campaign trail.

  • "We need to be doing a lot more to take on corporate power, to break up a lot of these monopolies that are rolling up — Big Pharma, insurance, private equity entering the space of health care unchecked," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told NBC. "I think there's a lot here for us to really dig in on, to work on."

What we're watching: Whether Republicans take Trump's advice to go on offense by making insurance companies the enemy in the final months before the midterms.

  • Democrats also will have to rely on more than partisan attacks and lay out a credible reform agenda and how they plan to take on corruption and hold special interests accountable, Lake Research Partners said.
item.content:encoded:
Campaigning on health care used to mean talking about coverage or costs. Now, in the run-up to the midterms, it's just as likely to focus on "corruption."

The big picture: Candidates are accusing primary or general election opponents of being in the pockets of drugmakers, insurers and other powerful health interests, to the detriment of voters.

  • It's a strategy that plays into affordability concerns and voter anger at the health system — but frequently avoids addressing what about the system needs fixing.
  • "Voters want leaders to lower everyday costs and firmly believe that will require taking on political corruption, corporate power and special interests' influence," public opinion firm Lake Research Partners wrote last month in a survey of attitudes about affordability and accountability.

Zoom in: That thinking is influencing the tone of one of the most competitive House races in the country, in Iowa's 1st Congressional District. GOP Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democrat Christina Bohannan, along with their surrogates, have accused each other of caving to big health insurers and undermining patient care.

  • In Michigan, Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed called his Republican opponent Mike Rogers a "pharma lobbyist," prompting Rogers' campaign to send a cease-and-desist letter and threaten legal action.
  • Charges of coziness with health industries also are surfacing in key Senate races in New Hampshire and Nebraska.
  • And some democratic socialists have played up drug and insurer donations to incumbents in primary challenges, as was the case when Melat Kiros knocked off 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado's 1st Congressional District.

Between the lines: Polling shows medical costs are the public's top economic worry.

  • Democratic challengers are trying to leverage that sentiment by focusing attention on opponents' campaign contributions, while Republicans tend to key on Democratic policies they say are handouts to certain industries.
  • The Lake Research Partners survey, commissioned by the progressive PAC Indivisible Action, found voters respond to the idea that rising costs stem primarily from corporate greed, corrupt CEOs and price gouging instead of government spending and waste.
  • "Voters aren't just concerned about the economy today; they are fed up with the resulting unfairness of a rigged system," it stated. "They see insiders, politicians, and corporations with too much power and elected leaders prioritizing their interests while ordinary people pay the cost."

Flashback: GOP lawmakers in Congress and outside conservative groups portrayed the Affordable Care Act as a profit-making machine for health insurers last year as they rallied to allow the expiration of pandemic-era enhanced subsidies.

  • A recent NPR analysis of YouTube ads found Republican candidates are now trying to get ahead of criticism of the subsidy expiration, and of health spending cuts in last year's sweeping reconciliation bill, by focusing on fraud in Medicaid, rural hospitals and affordability.
  • But Democrats think they can pin more health care cost issues on Republicans — and are highlighting policies in the reconciliation bill they say upended millions of lives and widened gaps in care.
  • Some are also criticizing President Trump's drug pricing deals, saying they really delivered big pharmaceutical companies tax breaks, regulatory relief and other perks.

What's next: House Democrats have already vowed to reverse the Medicaid cuts in the reconciliation bill and restore the enhanced ACA subsidies. But there's an added oversight component some are talking up on the campaign trail.

  • "We need to be doing a lot more to take on corporate power, to break up a lot of these monopolies that are rolling up — Big Pharma, insurance, private equity entering the space of health care unchecked," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told NBC. "I think there's a lot here for us to really dig in on, to work on."

What we're watching: Whether Republicans take Trump's advice to go on offense by making insurance companies the enemy in the final months before the midterms.

  • Democrats also will have to rely on more than partisan attacks and lay out a credible reform agenda and how they plan to take on corruption and hold special interests accountable, Lake Research Partners said.

item.title: How extreme heat is rewriting the job of state government
item.description:
As climate change makes extreme heat more frequent and dangerous, states are building systems to manage a hazard they weren't historically built to handle.

The big picture: In a growing number of states, officials are appointing heat officers, writing statewide plans, setting worker protections, funding cooling infrastructure, and coordinating responses across agencies.

Driving the news: July was the hottest month ever measured in the contiguous U.S., with every Lower 48 state above its 20th-century average.

  • The speed at which states have ramped up their response to extreme heat has been "stunning," V. Kelly Turner, associate director of heat research at the UCLA Luskin Center for Innovation, told Axios.
  • "Heat's everywhere, but it's sort of fallen through the cracks," said Turner, a professor of urban planning at UCLA. "If everyone's responsible, no one's responsible."

Part of the problem, she said, is that heat historically hasn't carried the same obvious property damage price tag as disasters such as floods and wildfires, so it can attract less government funding.

  • "Heat's already competing with all these other climate problems, and it doesn't have its own home; it doesn't have its own budget," she said.

Context: Massachusetts announced in August that it became the first East Coast state and second in the nation after Arizona to appoint a heat resilience officer.

  • The state has warmed by nearly 3.5°F in the past century.
  • Massachusetts Department of Public Health data shows there were nearly 1,500 heat-related emergency room visits last year.
  • Heat resilience officer Katie Schlick told Axios that 1 in 5 Massachusetts public schools lacks air conditioning. Sending kids home affects their learning, she said.

State of play: Arizona's 2024 heat plan created its chief heat officer role to coordinate heat-response efforts across agencies. It also expanded heat-relief resources and deployed mobile solar-powered cooling centers made from shipping containers.

  • Visits to two cooling centers at the Arizona Capitol rose 59% in summer 2025 from a year earlier, according to the state.

California has no official with such a title, but Turner said "we do have an office that is dedicated to extreme heat and a dedicated funding program that's putting a lot of money into the hands of communities to work on the problem."

  • California's 2022 Extreme Heat Action Plan established what officials called the state's first "all-of-government framework" for extreme heat.
  • Its updated 2026 plan spans public health, emergency response, housing, infrastructure, energy and worker protections.
  • A separate law will require cities and counties to address extreme heat hazards when they next update certain general plan elements on or after Jan. 1, 2028. Turner said that ultimately means "every single community" will have a clause "that says here's how we're addressing heat."

What we're watching: Schlick's initial goals for Massachusetts include reducing heat-related school closures through more cooling, building local heat-planning capacity, creating safer workplaces, and planting more trees.

  • The state has identified "heat equity communities" where less tree cover, shade and green space leave residents particularly exposed, Schlick said.

Schlick doesn't know whether she'll have dedicated funding for heat initiatives and expects to draw on broader resilience investments and existing programs and partnerships.

  • She wants to better quantify heat's costs — including lost work and wages, ER visits, and insurance costs — and measure which interventions are cost-effective.

The bottom line: "It's very early days in terms of heat governance," Turner said, as states figure out what an effective response looks like.

Go deeper: How Phoenix's chief heat officer is combating rising temperatures

item.title: Exclusive poll: GOP's gains among Latinos fade in House battlegrounds
item.description:
Data: Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision; Table: Russell Contreras/Axios

Democrats have gained sharply with Latino voters in some of the country's most competitive House districts since 2024, a new Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision poll shared exclusively with Axios shows.

Why it matters: President Trump came close to erasing Democrats' longtime advantage among Latinos in the last presidential election. Now, with control of Congress at stake and Trump's approval ratings hitting new lows, that breakthrough appears to have eroded.

  • Coming out of the 2024 election, Republicans hoped Trump's near-parity with Democrats among Latinos in 2024 would harden into a lasting political realignment favoring the GOP.
  • Instead, this poll and surveys earlier this year suggest that the nation's fastest-growing swing electorate is moving left, as anger at high prices and Trump's immigration policies appear to be giving Democrats an opening.

By the numbers: Democrats are gaining ground with Latino voters across a survey of 17 competitive House districts, opening a 58%-35% lead on the generic congressional ballot, according to the Hart Research for TelevisaUnivision poll.

  • That 23-point margin is double the 11-point edge Kamala Harris held over Trump in the same sample's self-reported 2024 vote.
  • Among Spanish-language media consumers, Democrats lead the 2026 generic ballot by 14 points, compared with a 1-point Trump edge in the group's self-reported 2024 vote.

Zoom in: In three Texas congressional districts — one on the Mexico border, another in suburban Fort Worth and another in the Austin-San Antonio corridor — Latino voters went from a self-reported 44-44 split in the 2024 presidential race to 56-36 in Democrats' favor today.

  • In Florida, Latino voters in two swing districts have gone from Trump +1 to Democrat +13 in the same period, the poll found.

The intrigue: 11% of Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now support Democratic congressional candidates.

State of play: Overall, Trump is deeply underwater with Latino voters in these battleground districts.

  • 63% disapprove of his overall job performance, compared with 36% who approve.
  • 65% disapprove of Trump's handling of prices and the cost of living, while 62% disapprove of his administration's immigration enforcement and deportations.
  • That marks a striking reversal from 2024, when Trump's gains with Latino voters helped produce the most racially diverse Republican presidential coalition in decades.

What they're saying: "Latino voters aren't locked into one party. They're paying close attention and making decisions based on who shows up for them, and how they're showing up," TelevisaUnivision Senior Vice President Kate Coleman tells Axios.

  • Aileen Cardona-Arroyo, a partner at Hart Research, tells Axios the survey showed Spanish language media is critical for engaging Latino voters in 2026 competitive congressional races.

Trump's immigration crackdown appears to have run into a wall with these voters — without producing a wholesale rejection of strict border enforcement.

  • ICE has a 64% unfavorable rating, including 65% among Latino independents.

Zoom out: The economy still outranks immigration as Latino voters' top concern, the survey indicates.

  • Democrats hold an advantage on the issue that helped Trump make gains among Latinos two years ago: 62% trust Democrats in Congress more to lower prices, versus 36% who trust Republicans more.

Methodology: The 2026 Latino Battleground survey included 1,500 Latino registered voters in 17 battleground congressional districts and was conducted Aug. 6-17, 2026, by Hart Research for TelevisaUnivision.

  • The margin of sampling error is ±2,5 percentage points for Latino adults at the 95% confidence level.

item.title: "Voters don't trust Jeffries": Democratic leader faces impending fight with the left
item.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) faces mounting behind-the-scenes frustration from progressive lawmakers and candidates that's likely to burst into public view after the midterm elections.

Why it matters: Unless Democrats win a big enough House majority in November to govern without the progressive wing, a Speaker Jeffries would have to contend with the left flank's demands.

An influx of Democratic Socialists of America-aligned members in January will compound latent distrust of Jeffries that's festering in some corners of the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

  • "He's got a lot of people mad at him," a senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of sensitive private discussions, told Axios.
  • Mai Vang, a progressive House candidate in Northern California, told Axios: "Voters don't trust Jeffries."

Driving the news: Jeffries has made several recent moves that left Progressive Caucus members fuming, according to multiple lawmakers, candidates and aides.

  • Medicare for All: Jeffries said on NBC's "Meet the Press" last month that Medicare for All is "not legislation ... that I support." He said in a later radio interview that he supports universal coverage, but there are "different paths" to get there.
  • Kushner meeting: Jeffries' sit-down with President Trump's son-in-law rankled progressive groups. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told reporters: "I don't know what that was about."
  • Rule change: A proposal to penalize members who don't pay their dues to the party's campaign arm, or who break with leadership on procedural votes, was seen by progressives as a preemptive attempt to cut off dissent from the left.

Combine this with long-standing progressive skepticism toward Jeffries, and you get all the ingredients for internal turmoil come Jan. 3.

  • "Constituents have shared with me that House Democrats need to replace Jeffries," said Vang, who's running in the Sacramento area. "That's something I've heard from voters."
  • A senior Progressive Caucus member told Axios they "consistently hear from constituents how displeased they are with the Democratic leadership, including Leader Jeffries."

Between the lines: Sitting congressional progressives have largely held their fire against Jeffries over the last two years. That may change after Election Day on Nov. 3.

  • Said the senior House progressive: "His latest comments and actions put members with dissatisfied constituents in a difficult position — do we represent our constituents or defend his leadership?"
  • The frustration is "bigger than the new crop of folks," a second senior House progressive said.
  • A third told Axios: "Democrats nationally want to see big changes, and that's what the caucus is going to be responding to."

Zoom in: Medicare for All is proving to be the most persistent sticking point for progressives, who say they're not going to drop the issue despite Jeffries' stated opposition.

  • Ocasio-Cortez told Axios: "The fact is, the majority of the Democratic caucus supports Medicare for All ... That, of course, is a dynamic that will be part of an ongoing conversation."
  • Said Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.): "We all deserve ... a health care system that everybody can afford, and we'll just keep fighting for that."
  • A fourth House progressive, granted anonymity to speak bluntly, said they "don't fucking get" Jeffries' refusal to support Medicare for All given that the party base has moved "very clearly to the left on so many issues."

Jeffries has stressed that his lack of support for Medicare for All is more about maintaining his neutrality as party leader than specific opposition to the policy itself.

  • Jeffries, a former Progressive Caucus member, had been a co-sponsor of Medicare for All legislation until he became leader in 2022.
  • "Consistent with what other leaders or speakers have done, when it comes to major pieces of legislation, we [as House minority leader] let the [House Democratic] caucus work out its will to try to actually get to a consensus position," he said in the radio interview last month.

Brad Lander, the progressive former New York City comptroller who unseated Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.) in June, pointed to Israel as another likely area of division between progressives and leadership.

  • "We don't want to send additional military aid to Israel while it continues a policy that I do believe is genocide," he said in an interview. "Those of us that ran on that platform, of course, will make our voices heard loud and clear in internal debates and conversations."

Yes, but: A fifth Progressive Caucus member acknowledged that while "there is frustration," Jeffries has been addressing internal dissent in real time.

  • "People reach out to him, and they have good conversations, and they move forward," the lawmaker said. "We try to hash things out immediately, and he's really open to having those conversations. He's spoken to a lot of people."

The bottom line: Watch what happens on Nov. 4, the day after Election Day.

  • "When we win the majority, we'll know we have won it with a huge amount of progressive energy," said Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar (D-Texas).
  • Progressive members, he said, "will make sure our party better holds the line on key progressive issues."

item.title: Zelensky to Axios: U.S. exploring Russia-Ukraine winter de-escalation steps
item.description:
The U.S. is exploring whether Ukraine and Russia could take steps to de-escalate the war during the winter while restarting negotiations toward a broader peace agreement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview Monday.

Why it matters: The Ukrainian president believes the weeks before winter offer a window for diplomacy. While Zelensky said he's convinced Russian President Vladimir Putin is counting on another brutal winter to weaken Ukraine, he added that Putin doesn't want to antagonize the U.S. president ahead of the midterm elections.

  • "My feeling [is] that Putin needs Trump," Zelensky said. "He doesn't want ... to upset him."
  • Zelensky said that even if Putin doesn't want to de-escalate, he could be pressured by the Trump administration to do so.
  • When asked whether Putin might want to give Trump a diplomatic win before the U.S. elections, Zelensky replied: "Yeah."

Driving the news: Zelensky met in Kyiv on Sunday with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. It was their first visit to Ukraine since Trump started his second term.

  • Kushner and Witkoff traveled to Kyiv after holding a three-hour meeting with Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday.
  • Zelensky said the message he received from the U.S. envoys was that "the Russians are ready to negotiate."
  • He remains skeptical, however, because Russia's actions on the battlefield and its recent escalation of attacks don't demonstrate a willingness to compromise.
  • But Zelensky said his understanding after the U.S. envoys' trip is that Putin is "ready to discuss" ideas for moving negotiations forward.

Behind the scenes: Zelensky said the U.S. envoys came to Moscow and Kyiv primarily to "unblock" the diplomatic process, but also brought some new ideas.

  • He declined to disclose all the details but said some of the discussions involved potential de-escalation steps from Russia and Ukraine ahead of and during the winter.
  • "There are ideas around energy [facilities] and around grain [shipments], around electricity [facilities] and around oil and gas [exports]. We have different interests, Russia and we," Zelensky said.
  • Asked whether the emerging U.S. approach involves both restarting negotiations and trying to reach understandings that would allow Ukraine and Russia to get through the winter without a major escalation, Zelensky said that interpretation was "very close to the reality of these conversations."
  • He described the first objective as resuming negotiations and the second as trying to make the coming winter different from previous ones, when Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure heightened the war.
  • The goal, he said, would be to find steps before or during the winter "which can bring [the] sides closer to the peace."

Yes, but: U.S. officials say they don't know if it will be possible to address the interests of both Russia and Ukraine ahead of winter. Countless previous attempts to reach ceasefires or pause strikes on energy facilities have failed.

What to watch: Zelensky said the U.S. team is expected to brief Trump and then continue consultations with Ukrainian and European officials.

State of play: Zelensky said the U.S. also supports a separate "winter package" for Ukraine that would include air defense and energy assistance.

  • "It's not only about missiles," Zelensky said. "It's also about LNG [liquefied natural gas] ... and it's also about steps of de-escalation."

The big picture: Zelensky believes Putin is counting on the winter to inflict enough damage on Ukraine to force Kyiv into further concessions.

  • "Russia really thinks that this winter can help them to break us," Zelensky said.
  • He said Moscow hopes a major winter offensive and attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure will deliver a "strong kick" after which Ukraine will become "more compromising."
  • Zelensky stressed that Ukraine has already made all the compromises it can and that any diplomatic process would also need security guarantees and an economic support package.
  • Zelensky also pointed out that Russia faces its own risks heading into the winter months. Ukraine, he said, can also hit Russia economically. "When they attacked our electricity, we blocked their possibility to sell oil and gas," he said. He also warned that disruptions to agricultural exports could drive up global food prices and cause food insecurity.

What's next: Zelensky said Ukraine wants to use September and October to restart a diplomatic process and suggested the UN General Assembly in New York later this month as a possible venue for further U.S.-Ukraine talks.

  • He said there is also the possibility of another trilateral U.S.-Ukraine-Russia negotiation session, though no decision has been made.
  • "We have this September, October to find any way to speak," Zelensky said. "Without dialogue … we will not have [a] result."
  • "I think that President Trump can find a way to [a] real beginning of the process of negotiating before [the] cold winter," he added.

Reality check: Zelensky said Ukraine would need to remain militarily strong throughout any diplomatic process and argued that Kyiv is currently in a better position on the battlefield than it was previously despite shortages in its air defense and continued Russian drone and missile attacks.

  • He also called for additional U.S. sanctions on Russia, describing them as a key source of leverage in any negotiations.
  • "Putin needs money," Zelensky said. "Putin wants money to continue the war."
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. is exploring whether Ukraine and Russia could take steps to de-escalate the war during the winter while restarting negotiations toward a broader peace agreement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview Monday.

Why it matters: The Ukrainian president believes the weeks before winter offer a window for diplomacy. While Zelensky said he's convinced Russian President Vladimir Putin is counting on another brutal winter to weaken Ukraine, he added that Putin doesn't want to antagonize the U.S. president ahead of the midterm elections.

  • "My feeling [is] that Putin needs Trump," Zelensky said. "He doesn't want ... to upset him."
  • Zelensky said that even if Putin doesn't want to de-escalate, he could be pressured by the Trump administration to do so.
  • When asked whether Putin might want to give Trump a diplomatic win before the U.S. elections, Zelensky replied: "Yeah."

Driving the news: Zelensky met in Kyiv on Sunday with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. It was their first visit to Ukraine since Trump started his second term.

  • Kushner and Witkoff traveled to Kyiv after holding a three-hour meeting with Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday.
  • Zelensky said the message he received from the U.S. envoys was that "the Russians are ready to negotiate."
  • He remains skeptical, however, because Russia's actions on the battlefield and its recent escalation of attacks don't demonstrate a willingness to compromise.
  • But Zelensky said his understanding after the U.S. envoys' trip is that Putin is "ready to discuss" ideas for moving negotiations forward.

Behind the scenes: Zelensky said the U.S. envoys came to Moscow and Kyiv primarily to "unblock" the diplomatic process, but also brought some new ideas.

  • He declined to disclose all the details but said some of the discussions involved potential de-escalation steps from Russia and Ukraine ahead of and during the winter.
  • "There are ideas around energy [facilities] and around grain [shipments], around electricity [facilities] and around oil and gas [exports]. We have different interests, Russia and we," Zelensky said.
  • Asked whether the emerging U.S. approach involves both restarting negotiations and trying to reach understandings that would allow Ukraine and Russia to get through the winter without a major escalation, Zelensky said that interpretation was "very close to the reality of these conversations."
  • He described the first objective as resuming negotiations and the second as trying to make the coming winter different from previous ones, when Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure heightened the war.
  • The goal, he said, would be to find steps before or during the winter "which can bring [the] sides closer to the peace."

Yes, but: U.S. officials say they don't know if it will be possible to address the interests of both Russia and Ukraine ahead of winter. Countless previous attempts to reach ceasefires or pause strikes on energy facilities have failed.

What to watch: Zelensky said the U.S. team is expected to brief Trump and then continue consultations with Ukrainian and European officials.

State of play: Zelensky said the U.S. also supports a separate "winter package" for Ukraine that would include air defense and energy assistance.

  • "It's not only about missiles," Zelensky said. "It's also about LNG [liquefied natural gas] ... and it's also about steps of de-escalation."

The big picture: Zelensky believes Putin is counting on the winter to inflict enough damage on Ukraine to force Kyiv into further concessions.

  • "Russia really thinks that this winter can help them to break us," Zelensky said.
  • He said Moscow hopes a major winter offensive and attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure will deliver a "strong kick" after which Ukraine will become "more compromising."
  • Zelensky stressed that Ukraine has already made all the compromises it can and that any diplomatic process would also need security guarantees and an economic support package.
  • Zelensky also pointed out that Russia faces its own risks heading into the winter months. Ukraine, he said, can also hit Russia economically. "When they attacked our electricity, we blocked their possibility to sell oil and gas," he said. He also warned that disruptions to agricultural exports could drive up global food prices and cause food insecurity.

What's next: Zelensky said Ukraine wants to use September and October to restart a diplomatic process and suggested the UN General Assembly in New York later this month as a possible venue for further U.S.-Ukraine talks.

  • He said there is also the possibility of another trilateral U.S.-Ukraine-Russia negotiation session, though no decision has been made.
  • "We have this September, October to find any way to speak," Zelensky said. "Without dialogue … we will not have [a] result."
  • "I think that President Trump can find a way to [a] real beginning of the process of negotiating before [the] cold winter," he added.

Reality check: Zelensky said Ukraine would need to remain militarily strong throughout any diplomatic process and argued that Kyiv is currently in a better position on the battlefield than it was previously despite shortages in its air defense and continued Russian drone and missile attacks.

  • He also called for additional U.S. sanctions on Russia, describing them as a key source of leverage in any negotiations.
  • "Putin needs money," Zelensky said. "Putin wants money to continue the war."
